why_companies_ask_this.title: Why Linked Lists Have The Most Blind 75 Problems In Level 1
why_companies_ask_this.content: Linked list problems are the purest test of pointer manipulation skill. Every operation requires tracking multiple references simultaneously, updating them in the correct order, and handling edge cases that only appear at boundaries. Companies use linked list problems to filter candidates who can reason about references — a skill that directly transfers to tree and graph pointer manipulation, memory management in C/C++, and building production data structures. LRU Cache specifically appears at every senior FAANG interview because it combines pointer manipulation (DLL) with data structure composition (DLL + hash map) and demonstrates system design thinking — the exact combination that separates senior engineers from junior engineers.

company_specific.insight: Amazon's SDE-2 and SDE-3 interviews almost always include LRU Cache or a variant (LFU Cache, K most recently accessed). The expected answer requires explicit mention of both hash map and doubly linked list with O(1) justification for each. Candidates who answer 'array + sort' or 'single map with timestamps' do not pass.

Google uses Merge K Sorted Lists as a technical screen filter for L4+. The divide-and-conquer O(N log k) proof is specifically asked: 'Prove your solution is O(N log k) and not O(kN).' Candidates who cannot explain why the recursion tree has log k levels and O(N) work per level do not pass the technical bar.

Indian product companies test Floyd's cycle detection as a favourite linked list problem because the algorithm requires understanding a non-obvious proof. The question 'Why does resetting one pointer to head and advancing both at speed 1 find the cycle start?' differentiates candidates who memorised the algorithm from those who understand it.

lessons.title: Singly Linked List Structure
lessons.objective: Understand the singly linked list structure at the memory level, implement a Node and LinkedList class, and know exactly when a linked list is preferable to an array.
concepts: Node structure: value and next pointer
Head pointer as the entry point to the list
Null-terminated tail: last node's next is null
Traversal: follow next pointers until null — O(n)
Access by index: O(n) — no direct address calculation
No wasted capacity: nodes allocated individually
Non-contiguous memory: cache locality tradeoff
When linked list beats array: frequent insert/delete at head, unknown size
lessons.explanation: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. The list is accessed through a head pointer that points to the first node. The last node's next pointer is null, marking the end. Unlike arrays, linked list nodes are not stored contiguously in memory — each node is allocated separately and can live anywhere in the heap. This means index-based access requires traversing from the head one node at a time: O(n). There is no base_address + i * element_size shortcut. The tradeoff: what linked lists lose in random access they gain in dynamic sizing and O(1) insert or delete at the head without shifting elements. Arrays waste space by pre-allocating capacity; linked lists allocate exactly one node per element with no over-allocation. The pointer overhead (8 bytes per node for the next pointer on a 64-bit system) is the cost. For a list of 4-byte integers, each node uses 12 bytes instead of 4 — a 3x memory overhead compared to an array.
lessons.analogy: A linked list is a scavenger hunt. Each clue (node) gives you one piece of information (value) and the location of the next clue (next pointer). To find clue number 7, you must start from clue 1 and follow every pointer in sequence. You cannot skip ahead. An array is a numbered grid of post boxes — you go directly to box 7 without looking at any other box. The scavenger hunt is slower to access but trivially easy to extend — just hide a new clue anywhere and update the previous clue's location pointer.

code_example.explanation: prepend is O(1) because it only updates the head pointer and the new node's next pointer. append is O(n) because it must traverse to the tail. This asymmetry is a fundamental property of singly linked lists without a tail pointer. Adding a tail pointer as a class field makes append O(1) but requires updating it on every operation that modifies the tail.

common_mistakes: Losing the head pointer during traversal — always use a separate curr variable to traverse; never move head itself or you lose access to the entire list
Not handling the empty list case — operations like append, delete, and find must check if head is null before dereferencing; null pointer dereference is the most common linked list bug

Confusing the node reference with the node's value — curr is a reference to a ListNode object; curr.val is the integer value; curr.next is the reference to the next node; keeping these distinct prevents most pointer logic errors
lessons.interview_relevance: Linked list problems make up a significant portion of Blind 75. Interviewers specifically use them to test pointer manipulation skills because pointer bugs are immediately visible and hard to hide. A candidate who can implement prepend, append, and traversal from scratch in 3 minutes demonstrates fundamental CS comfort that signals readiness for harder problems.
lessons.mini_challenge: Build a LinkedList class with a tail pointer so that both prepend and append are O(1). Add a get(index) method that returns the value at a given index in O(n). Add a size property. Then implement a printReverse() method that prints the list in reverse order using recursion (no extra data structures). State the time and space complexity of printReverse.

visual_explanation.description: Draw two diagrams side by side. Left: Array [0,1,2,3] stored contiguously at addresses 1000,1004,1008,1012. Show formula: address = 1000 + (i×4). Arrow to arr[2] goes directly to 1008. Label O(1) direct access. Right: Linked list nodes scattered. head→[0|→2500], [2500:1|→4100], [4100:2|→600], [600:3|null]. Arrow to 3rd node goes head→1st→2nd→3rd. Label O(n) traversal. Below: Memory overhead comparison table — Array: 4 bytes/element, Linked List: 12 bytes/element (4 val + 8 ptr). Callout: 'Tail pointer makes append O(1) — draw a direct arrow from tail to last node, bypassing traversal'.

interview_war_story.story: The interviewer asked the candidate to implement a linked list. The candidate wrote append correctly but moved head forward during traversal: 'while(head.next) head = head.next;'. After building the list they called toArray() and got only the last element. The interviewer asked 'What does your list look like now?' The candidate traced and saw: head now points to the last node — all previous nodes are unreachable. 'I destroyed my head pointer during traversal.' The fix: always use curr = this.head and traverse curr, never head.
interview_war_story.lesson: Never advance head during traversal. head is your only entry point to the list. Use a separate curr = head and advance curr. This is the most common linked list bug that immediately fails every subsequent operation.

questions.question: Why is accessing the 5th element of a linked list O(n) but accessing the 5th element of an array O(1)?
options: Linked lists are slower data structures
Arrays compute the address directly as base + index × size — O(1). Linked lists have no address formula; you must follow next pointers from head one at a time — O(n).
Linked lists store data differently
Arrays have a special CPU cache
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements contiguously — address = base + (i × element_size), one arithmetic operation. Linked list nodes scatter across memory; the only way to reach node 5 is to follow head.next.next.next.next — four pointer dereferences regardless of where nodes live.

questions.question: What is the memory overhead of a singly linked list node storing a 4-byte integer on a 64-bit system?
options: 4 bytes — same as array
8 bytes — just the pointer
12 bytes — 4 bytes value + 8 bytes next pointer (3x overhead vs array)
16 bytes
questions.explanation: Each node needs: 4 bytes for the integer value + 8 bytes for the next pointer on a 64-bit system = 12 bytes per node. An array stores the same integer in 4 bytes. Linked list uses 3x the memory per element. This overhead is the cost of dynamic sizing and O(1) head insertion.

questions.question: You have a curr variable traversing a linked list. Calling curr = curr.next moves to the next node. What is the worst thing you can do to head during traversal?
options: Read head.val
Set head = curr — this loses the entry point to the list; you can no longer access nodes before curr
Call head.next
Print head.val
questions.explanation: head is the only entry point to the list. If you advance head during traversal, all nodes before the current position become unreachable — they cannot be garbage collected and are permanently lost from your access. Always use a separate curr variable for traversal; never move head.

append: if(!this.head){this.head=this.tail=node;}else{this.tail.next=node;this.tail=node;} printReverse: if(!node)return; this.printReverse(node.next); console.log(node.val);

theory_mcq.question: What is the fundamental structural difference between a linked list and an array in memory, and what are the key consequences of this difference?
options: Linked lists and arrays use identical memory layouts; the only difference is naming

Arrays store elements in CONTIGUOUS memory (adjacent addresses), enabling O(1) index access via direct address calculation; linked lists store nodes at NON-CONTIGUOUS, scattered memory locations connected only by explicit next pointers, making index access O(n) (must follow the chain) but enabling O(1) prepend/head-insert without shifting anything
Linked lists always use less memory than arrays
Arrays cannot store more than one type of data, while linked lists can
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's core trade-off: arrays use contiguous memory enabling direct address computation for any index (O(1) access), while linked list nodes scatter in memory connected via pointers — this makes linked lists poor for random access (O(n) traversal required) but ideal for O(1) head operations, since no shifting of other elements is ever needed.

theory_mcq.question: Why is `append` O(n) while `prepend` is O(1) in the lesson's singly linked list implementation?
options: Both operations are O(n); the lesson's complexity claims are incorrect

Prepend only updates the `head` pointer to a new node (O(1), no traversal), while append must walk the ENTIRE chain from head to the last node (O(n)) before linking the new node — a linked list with only a head pointer has no O(1) shortcut to the tail
append is O(1) and prepend is O(n); the question has the complexities reversed
Both are O(1) when using JavaScript's built-in linked list class
theory_mcq.explanation: prepend sets `this.head = new ListNode(val, this.head)` — one operation, O(1). append must traverse `while (curr.next) curr = curr.next` from the head to find the tail — this traversal is O(n). A tail pointer would make append O(1), but the lesson's implementation doesn't maintain one.

theory_mcq.question: Per the lesson, when does a linked list beat an array? What specific use cases make its trade-offs worthwhile?
options: Linked lists always beat arrays; arrays have no advantages

Linked lists are preferable for frequent insert/delete at the HEAD (O(1) vs O(n) array shift) and when the required size is UNKNOWN at allocation time (no wasted capacity or costly resizing) — but they lose for random access by index, cache-heavy workloads, and when elements are rarely inserted or deleted
Linked lists are only useful for storing exactly 3 elements
Linked lists beat arrays only when sorting is required
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's exact stated benefits: 'When linked list beats array: frequent insert/delete at head, unknown size' — O(1) head operations without shifting, and individually-allocated nodes avoiding upfront capacity commitment or costly resize operations, are the primary advantages that justify linked lists' O(n) random access trade-off.

logic_mcq.question: Trace: `list.append(1); list.append(2); list.append(3); list.prepend(0);`. What does `list.toArray()` return, and what is `list.size`?
options: [1,2,3,0] and size=4 — prepend adds to the end
[0,1,2,3] and size=4 — append adds 1,2,3 to the tail one-by-one, then prepend(0) inserts a new head before 1, producing the chain 0->1->2->3; confirmed by direct execution
[0,1,2,3] and size=3 — prepend doesn't increment size
[0,3,2,1] and size=4 — append reverses order
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact output, confirmed by direct execution: three appends build the chain 1->2->3 (each walk to the current tail and links a new node), then prepend(0) sets head to a new node pointing to the old head (1), producing 0->1->2->3; toArray() follows next pointers to produce [0,1,2,3] and size is correctly incremented to 4 across all four operations.

logic_mcq.question: How many pointer dereferences does it take to access 'node 3' (value 3) in a 4-node linked list starting from head, and what does this reveal about the O(n) access cost?
options: Zero dereferences — linked lists support O(1) direct access like arrays

Three pointer dereferences: head.next (reaches node 1), .next (reaches node 2), .next (reaches node 3) — the lesson's own memory diagram confirms this: 'Access node 3: head.next.next.next — 3 pointer dereferences'; in general, accessing the kth node requires k pointer dereferences, directly reflecting the O(n) access cost
One dereference — accessing any node always costs O(1)
Four dereferences — you must always traverse the entire list first
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit memory diagram: 'Access node 3: head.next.next.next — 3 pointer dereferences' — to reach the node at position k (0-indexed), exactly k next-pointer dereferences are required (no shortcut formula exists as with arrays), which is what makes linked list access O(n) in the worst case.

syntax_mcq.question: In `constructor(val, next = null)` for ListNode, what does `next = null` accomplish as a default parameter?
options: It forces next to permanently be null and cannot be changed

It provides a DEFAULT value of null for the `next` parameter — when a node is constructed with only a value (e.g., `new ListNode(5)`), `next` automatically defaults to null, correctly representing a node with no successor (useful for tail nodes and newly-allocated nodes before linking); callers can override this default explicitly to set a specific successor immediately at construction time
It makes next a required parameter that must always be explicitly provided
null has no special meaning here; it's just an arbitrary sentinel value
syntax_mcq.explanation: The default parameter `next = null` means `new ListNode(5)` creates a standalone node with next=null (no successor), while `new ListNode(5, existingNode)` creates a node immediately linked to an existing successor — both usage patterns appear throughout the lesson's code, and the default prevents needing an explicit `null` argument for standalone nodes.

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: prepend: O(1). append: O(1) with tail pointer (vs O(n) without). deleteHead: O(1). find/toArray: O(n). The tail pointer addition makes append O(1) at the cost of one extra pointer to maintain.

hints.text: prepend: after making the new node the head, check if tail is null (empty list) and set tail to the new node if so.
append: if tail is null (empty list), set BOTH head and tail; otherwise link tail.next to the new node and advance tail.
deleteHead: after removing the head, check if head is now null (list became empty) and set tail to null in that case — both pointers must stay consistent.

lessons.title: Insert And Delete Operations
lessons.objective: Implement insert and delete at any position in a linked list with correct predecessor tracking, and understand why these operations are O(1) given the predecessor node.
concepts: Insert after a given node: O(1) pointer update
Insert at position k: O(k) traverse then O(1) update
Delete a specific node given its predecessor: O(1)
Delete by value: O(n) find predecessor then O(1) remove
Dummy head node: eliminates special cases for head deletion
The predecessor problem: singly linked list requires knowing the node before
Two-pointer predecessor tracking pattern
In-place list modification without creating new nodes
lessons.explanation: Insert and delete in a linked list are O(1) operations given the correct predecessor node, because they only update two or three pointers. Insert after node prev: create newNode, set newNode.next = prev.next, set prev.next = newNode. Two pointer updates, O(1). Delete node after prev: set prev.next = prev.next.next. One pointer update, O(1). The expensive part is finding the predecessor: traversing k nodes to reach the insertion or deletion position takes O(k). So insert or delete at position k is O(k) overall. The dummy head (sentinel node) is the cleanest technique for eliminating special cases when the head itself must be deleted. Without a dummy head, deleting the first node requires special-casing head = head.next. With a dummy head, the real head is just another node preceded by the dummy, so the same predecessor-based deletion works uniformly for all positions. Always use a dummy head in linked list problems that modify the list structure.
lessons.analogy: Insert in a linked list is like inserting a new wagon in a train. To insert after wagon 5, you detach the link between wagon 5 and wagon 6, hook the new wagon to wagon 5, and hook wagon 6 to the new wagon. Two hook changes, regardless of how long the train is. Finding wagon 5 requires walking the train from the locomotive, which takes time proportional to position.

code_example.explanation: deleteNode (deleting a node given only itself, not its predecessor) is a famous interview trick. Since singly linked lists cannot go backwards, you cannot find the predecessor. The workaround: overwrite the node's value with its successor's value, then delete the successor (which you can do because you have a reference to it). This effectively removes the target value from the list in O(1) without needing the predecessor.

common_mistakes: Not using a dummy head when the head itself might be deleted — without a dummy, you need an if-statement for head deletion that is easy to get wrong; the dummy head makes every deletion uniform

Advancing prev when deleting — after deleting prev.next, prev should NOT advance because prev.next now points to a different node that also needs to be checked; only advance prev when no deletion occurs

Losing the deleted node's next pointer before updating prev.next — in deleteAfter, prev.next = prev.next.next is safe because you do not need the intermediate node again; but in multi-step operations, save pointers before overwriting them
lessons.interview_relevance: The dummy head pattern appears in LeetCode #203 Remove Linked List Elements, #82 Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II, and #21 Merge Two Sorted Lists. Interviewers specifically look for dummy head usage because candidates who know it write cleaner code with fewer edge case bugs. Not using it signals unfamiliarity with standard linked list technique.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement removeAllOccurrences using the dummy head pattern. Then implement insertAtPosition(head, pos, val) that inserts val before position pos (0-indexed). Use a dummy head and a counter. Handle the case where pos is 0 (insert before the current head) and pos equals the list length (append). State the time complexity.

visual_explanation.description: Draw removeAllOccurrences on [1,2,6,3,6]. Show dummy→1→2→6→3→6→null with prev starting at dummy. At each step: prev | prev.next | action | list state. prev=dummy, prev.next=1: no delete, prev→1. prev=1, prev.next=2: no delete, prev→2. prev=2, prev.next=6: DELETE, prev.next→3. DO NOT advance prev. prev=2, prev.next=3: no delete, prev→3. prev=3, prev.next=6: DELETE, prev.next→null. Done. Result: [1,2,3]. Highlight in red that after each deletion, prev STAYS — do not advance. Contrast with a broken version that advances prev after deletion — show it skips the node after the deleted one.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was to remove all elements equal to a given value from a linked list. The candidate did not use a dummy head. Their code: if(head.val===val) head=head.next; Then a while loop for the rest. The interviewer said 'What if the entire list is [6,6,6] and you remove 6?' The candidate traced: first iteration moves head forward, but then the loop condition checks head which was already moved. The logic was broken for consecutive head deletions. The interviewer said 'Add a dummy node.' The candidate added it in 2 minutes and the code worked for all cases. 'The dummy node is not optional in linked list problems that modify the head — it is standard technique.'
interview_war_story.lesson: Use a dummy head whenever the head itself might be deleted or replaced. It makes head deletion identical to all other deletions, eliminating a class of edge-case bugs entirely.

questions.question: Given the predecessor node prev, what is the time complexity of deleting the next node?
options: O(n) — must traverse to the node to delete
O(1) — prev.next = prev.next.next skips the node in one pointer update
O(log n)
O(n) — must update all subsequent nodes
questions.explanation: With the predecessor in hand: prev.next = prev.next.next removes the target node in one pointer update — O(1). The expensive part is FINDING the predecessor (O(n) traversal), not the deletion itself. This is why linked list operations are stated as O(1) given the predecessor — it separates the traversal cost from the structural modification cost.

questions.question: Why use a dummy head node when implementing removeAllOccurrences?
options: It makes the code faster

Without a dummy, deleting the actual head node requires a special case (head = head.next). The dummy node makes the real head just another node with a predecessor (the dummy), so the same predecessor-based deletion logic handles all positions uniformly — no special cases.
Dummy nodes save memory
The algorithm does not work without a dummy
questions.explanation: Without dummy: if head.val === val, you must special-case head = head.next. With dummy: dummy.next points to the real head. The real head has a predecessor (the dummy). When head.val === val, prev.next = prev.next.next works exactly like any other deletion. The dummy eliminates the special case, making the code cleaner and less error-prone.

questions.question: In removeAllOccurrences, when should you NOT advance the prev pointer?
options: Never advance prev
When you delete prev.next — after deletion, prev.next points to a new (not-yet-examined) node. Advancing prev would skip examining that new node.
Always advance prev after checking
When prev.next is null
questions.explanation: When deleting: prev.next = prev.next.next skips the target. Now prev.next is a new node that may also need to be deleted. If you advance prev now, you skip examining this new node. Only advance prev when no deletion occurs — that ensures every node gets examined exactly once.

coding_quest.title: Remove All Occurrences And Insert At Position
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement removeAllOccurrences(head, val) using the dummy head pattern. Then implement insertAtPosition(head, pos, val) that inserts val before position pos (0-indexed). Use dummy head for both. Test removeAllOccurrences on [1,2,6,3,4,5,6] removing 6 → [1,2,3,4,5]. Test insertAtPosition on [1,2,3] pos=1 val=99 → [1,99,2,3].

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Advancing prev after deletion is the most common bug. After prev.next = prev.next.next, the new prev.next is an unexamined node — advancing prev now skips it. For input [6,6,6] removing 6: after first deletion next 6 is at prev.next. If you advance, you skip it.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n) time but wrong — skips consecutive duplicates

hints.text: removeAllOccurrences: in the deletion branch, do NOT advance prev — just set prev.next = prev.next.next. Only advance prev in the else branch (no deletion). insertAtPosition: loop i<pos times advancing curr. After the loop, curr is the predecessor. newNode.next = curr.next; curr.next = newNode.

Why not advance prev on deletion: after deletion, prev.next is a new unexamined node. It might also equal val. If you advance, you skip it. The dummy head handles pos=0 insert and val=head.val removal identically to all other cases.
removeAllOccurrences: if(prev.next.val===val)prev.next=prev.next.next; else prev=prev.next; insertAtPosition loop: for(let i=0;i<pos;i++) if(curr.next) curr=curr.next;

theory_mcq.question: Why is deleting a node from a singly linked list O(1) ONLY when given the PREDECESSOR node, rather than the target node itself?
options: Deleting a node is always O(1) regardless of which node reference you have

Deletion in a singly linked list works by updating the predecessor's `next` pointer to skip the target node (prev.next = prev.next.next) — without the predecessor, you'd have to traverse from the head to FIND the predecessor, which takes O(n); if only given the target node, there's no `prev` pointer to update since singly linked lists are unidirectional
You can always delete a node directly without knowing its predecessor
The O(1) only applies to deleting the tail, never the head
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's core 'predecessor problem': deletion rewrites `prev.next = prev.next.next`, and a singly linked list node only stores `next` (not `prev`) — so you MUST have the predecessor to perform O(1) deletion; finding it from scratch requires an O(n) traversal from head.

theory_mcq.question: What problem does the 'dummy head' pattern solve, and why is it used in `removeAllOccurrences`?
options: The dummy head is purely decorative with no functional purpose

The dummy head (a sentinel node placed before the real head) ELIMINATES the special case for head deletion — without it, deleting the first node requires separate logic (updating `this.head`) from deleting any other node; with a dummy head, the real head is just another node after the dummy, so the SAME `prev.next = prev.next.next` logic handles deletions uniformly at any position including the first real node
The dummy head is required by JavaScript syntax for linked list operations
The dummy head prevents memory leaks by holding deleted node references
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit explanation: 'Dummy head node: eliminates special cases for head deletion' — by making the dummy a permanent predecessor of the real head, head deletion becomes identical to mid-list deletion, so no if-branch is needed to check 'is this the first node?' at each step.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `removeAllOccurrences([1,2,6,3,4,5,6], 6)` per the lesson's own worked example. At what two steps does an actual deletion occur, and what does the resulting list look like?
options: Deletions occur at the first and last positions, and the result is [2,3,4,5]

Deletions occur when prev.next is the first 6 (after node 2) and the second 6 (after node 5) — first: prev=2, prev.next=6→set prev.next=3; second: prev=5, prev.next=6→set prev.next=null; result is [1,2,3,4,5], confirmed by direct execution
All six elements are deleted, leaving an empty list
Only the first 6 is deleted; the second requires a separate call
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace, confirmed by direct execution: the algorithm walks with a prev pointer, and when prev.next.val===6 it does NOT advance prev (since the next node might also be 6), only adjusting the pointer; two deletions occur (at the first and last 6) producing [1,2,3,4,5] as the final list.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson's `deleteNode(node)` trick copies `node.next.val` into `node.val` and sets `node.next = node.next.next`. Why can't this trick be applied to a TAIL node?
options: The trick works fine on tail nodes; the lesson's restriction is incorrect

The trick works by 'impersonating' the successor: copying the next node's value and deleting THAT next node instead of the current node — but a tail node has `node.next === null`, so `node.next.val` would be a null-pointer dereference (throwing an error), and there's no successor to copy; the tail can only be correctly deleted by updating its predecessor's next pointer
This trick only fails on tail nodes when the list has fewer than 3 elements
The trick fails because tail nodes store their value differently
logic_mcq.explanation: The lesson explicitly states: 'Assumes node is not the tail' — the trick relies on copying the NEXT node's value and then unlinking that next node, but a tail node has no next node (next===null), making the copy operation undefined and the skip impossible.

logic_mcq.question: In `removeAllOccurrences`, why does the loop NOT advance `prev` (i.e., `prev = prev.next` is skipped) when a deletion occurs?
options: This is a bug — prev should always advance on every iteration

After deleting a node (prev.next = prev.next.next), the NEW `prev.next` is a DIFFERENT node that hasn't been examined yet — advancing prev at this point would skip over this next node without checking whether IT also has the deletion value; by staying at the current prev position after a deletion, the algorithm correctly re-examines the new prev.next on the next iteration, handling consecutive identical values like [6,6] correctly
prev never advances regardless of whether a deletion occurs
Advancing prev only happens after the loop completes
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the key logic detail for correct multiple-deletion handling: when a node is deleted (prev.next = prev.next.next), what was previously prev.next.next becomes the new prev.next — this new node must be examined before advancing prev, since it might also match the deletion value (e.g., consecutive 6s). Advancing prev prematurely would skip this check.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const newNode = new ListNode(val, prev.next);` followed by `prev.next = newNode;`, why must `prev.next` be captured in the ListNode constructor BEFORE `prev.next` is overwritten?
options: The order doesn't matter; both lines can be written in any sequence

The insertAfter pattern requires the new node to point to what WAS prev's old successor BEFORE prev is updated to point to the new node — if `prev.next = newNode` were done first, `prev.next` would then refer to the new node itself, and passing `prev.next` to the ListNode constructor would create a self-loop; the constructor captures the OLD `prev.next` (the intended successor) BEFORE it's overwritten
ListNode constructors always ignore the `next` parameter
This order only matters for doubly linked lists, not singly linked ones
syntax_mcq.explanation: Insertion order matters critically: the new node must be initialized with a `next` pointer to the OLD successor (prev's current next) BEFORE prev's next pointer is updated to the new node; reversing the order would make `prev.next` point to the new (incomplete) node before it's finished being set up, breaking the chain.

lessons.title: Reverse A Linked List
lessons.objective: Reverse a singly linked list both iteratively with three pointers and recursively with the trust-the-recursion pattern, and extend to reversing a sublist.
concepts: Iterative reversal: prev, curr, next pointer dance
Three-pointer state machine: prev=null, curr=head initially
Loop invariant: nodes behind curr are reversed
Recursive reversal: trust that reversing the tail returns the new head
Connecting the reversed tail back to the current head
Reverse a sublist: positions left to right
Reverse in groups of k
Why reversal is O(n) time and O(1) iterative, O(n) recursive space
lessons.explanation: Reversing a linked list iteratively uses three pointers: prev (initially null), curr (initially head), and next (temporary). At each step: save curr.next before overwriting it, point curr.next backward to prev, advance prev to curr, advance curr to saved next. After the loop, prev points to the new head. The loop invariant: all nodes from the original head up to but not including curr have been reversed. When curr becomes null, all nodes are reversed and prev is the new head. Recursive reversal: for a list of length > 1, recursively reverse the sublist starting at head.next (trust this returns the new head with the tail now reversed). The original head.next is now the last node of the reversed tail. Set head.next.next = head (make the tail's last node point back to head) and set head.next = null (head is now the tail). The recursion depth is O(n) so space complexity is O(n) for the call stack.
lessons.analogy: Iterative reversal is like reversing a chain of people holding hands. You stand at the front (curr) and tell each person to stop holding the hand of the person in front and instead hold the hand of the person behind them (prev). After you pass through everyone, the last person (prev) is now at the front of the reversed chain. Three variables are needed: who you just processed (prev), who you are processing now (curr), and who is next in line (next, saved before you break the connection).

code_example.explanation: In reverseBetween, after the reversal loop, prev.next still points to the original left node, which is now the sublist tail. Setting prev.next.next = curr connects it to the node after right. Then prev.next = tail connects to the new sublist head (original right node). The order of these two assignments matters: if you set prev.next = tail first, you lose the reference to the original left node (now the sublist tail).

common_mistakes: Forgetting to save curr.next before overwriting curr.next = prev — once you set curr.next = prev, you lose access to the rest of the list; always save next = curr.next as the first line of the loop body
Returning curr instead of prev after the iterative loop — when the loop exits, curr is null (past the end); prev is the last node processed, which is the new head
Not setting head.next = null in the recursive reversal — without this, the original head still points to the second node creating a cycle; head must become the new tail with a null next pointer
lessons.interview_relevance: Reverse Linked List (#206) is Blind 75 and the most commonly asked linked list problem. Every interviewer expects both iterative and recursive solutions. Reverse Linked List II (#92, reverse sublist) and Reverse Nodes in k-Group (#25) are NeetCode 150 follow-ups. Being able to code the iterative reversal from memory in under 2 minutes is the baseline expectation.

State the time complexity O(n) and space complexity O(1).

visual_explanation.description: Draw the three-pointer iterative reversal on [1,2,3,4,5] as 5 rows, one per iteration. Each row: state of prev, curr, next + the list with arrows. Row 1: prev=null, curr=1, next=2. Arrow from 1 to null (reversed). Row 2: prev=1, curr=2, next=3. Arrow from 2 to 1. Row 3: prev=2, curr=3, next=4. Row 4: prev=3, curr=4, next=5. Row 5: prev=4, curr=5, next=null. Arrow from 5 to 4. Loop exits. Prev=5 is new head. Then separately draw reverseBetween [1,2,3,4,5] left=2 right=4: show the two steps — walk to predecessor of left (prev=node1), then reverse 3 nodes (2,3,4), then reconnect (1→4, 2→5).

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Reverse Nodes in k-Group. The candidate coded it but reversed prev.next and tail assignments in the reconnect step. Code: prev.next=tail; prev.next.next=curr. After setting prev.next=tail, prev.next now refers to tail, not the original sublist start. prev.next.next = curr correctly sets tail.next = curr — but the original sublist tail's .next was never updated. The list was broken. The interviewer asked them to trace through on paper. The candidate saw the bug immediately. Rule: set the sublist tail's next pointer BEFORE changing prev.next, because once prev.next changes you lose the reference to the sublist tail.
interview_war_story.lesson: In reversal reconnection, always set the sublist tail's next pointer FIRST (prev.next.next = curr), then update the predecessor's pointer (prev.next = tail). Swapping this order loses the sublist tail reference.

questions.question: In the iterative reversal, why must you save curr.next BEFORE setting curr.next = prev?
options: For performance

Once curr.next = prev is executed, the original next node is unreachable via curr. Saving next = curr.next first preserves the only reference to the rest of the list, allowing you to advance curr after the reversal step.
curr.next is read-only
The order does not matter
questions.explanation: curr.next = prev overwrites the next pointer. After this line, there is no way to reach the original next node via curr — the forward path is destroyed. If you did not save next = curr.next before this line, you permanently lose access to the rest of the list. Save first, modify second.

questions.question: After the iterative reversal loop exits (curr is null), what does prev point to?
options: null — the end of the list
The original head — unchanged
The new head — the last node of the original list, which is now first in the reversed list
The second node of the original list
questions.explanation: The loop advances prev to curr at each step. When curr becomes null (one past the end), prev is at the last node that was processed — the original last node. Since all pointers are now reversed, this original last node is the new head of the reversed list. Return prev, not curr.

questions.question: In the recursive reversal, why must you set head.next = null after head.next.next = head?
options: head.next = null is optional
Without it, head still points to the second node (head.next), creating a cycle: head→head.next and head.next.next→head. The list is circular and infinite. head.next = null makes head the new tail.
Performance optimisation
JavaScript garbage collection requires this
questions.explanation: After the recursive call returns, head.next.next = head creates a backward link from the second node to head. But head.next still points to the second node forward. This creates a cycle: head ↔ second node. Setting head.next = null breaks the forward link from head, making head the new tail (pointing to null) and eliminating the cycle.

reverseBetween reconnection order MATTERS: prev.next.next = curr must come FIRST (curr is the node after 'right'). Then prev.next = tail. If you do prev.next = tail first, you lose the reference to the sublist tail (originally prev.next), and you cannot set its .next pointer.
Recursive: head.next.next=head;head.next=null;return newHead. reverseBetween reconnect: prev.next.next=curr; prev.next=tail; (this order is mandatory — do not swap).

theory_mcq.question: Why does the iterative `reverseList` use THREE pointers (prev, curr, next), and what would go wrong if `next` were not saved before reversing `curr.next`?
options: Two pointers would work identically; the third is unnecessary

Without saving `next = curr.next` BEFORE executing `curr.next = prev`, the old forward pointer is PERMANENTLY LOST — `curr.next` is immediately overwritten to point backwards, making it impossible to advance `curr` to the next node in the original chain; `next` captures this forward reference before it's destroyed, allowing the algorithm to continue traversal even after reversing the current link
next is only needed for the first and last nodes, not intermediate ones
Three pointers are required by JavaScript syntax for while-loops
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the fundamental correctness concern for iterative reversal: reversing `curr.next = prev` destroys the original forward link — without first capturing `next = curr.next`, there's no way to advance `curr` after the reversal; the three-pointer dance (save, reverse, advance both prev and curr) is the minimal state needed to make one correct reversal step.

theory_mcq.question: In the recursive `reverseListRecursive`, after `const newHead = reverseListRecursive(head.next)` returns, `head.next` still points to the SECOND node (now the tail of the reversed sublist). Why does `head.next.next = head` correctly attach `head` to the end of the reversed sublist?
options: head.next.next = head is an error and would create a cycle

After recursively reversing head.next..tail, `head.next` is the node that was originally second — it's now the LAST node of the reversed tail sublist, since all pointers behind it are already reversed. Setting `head.next.next = head` makes this last-in-the-reversed-tail node point forward to `head`, correctly appending `head` to the reversed chain; then `head.next = null` makes `head` the new null-terminated tail
head.next doesn't change during the recursive call, so this line has no effect
This only works for lists of exactly 2 nodes
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the 'trust the recursion' argument applied to reversal: after reversing head.next..tail, head.next (the original second node) is at the END of the reversed sublist — by setting head.next.next = head and head.next = null, we're appending the original head as the new tail of an already-reversed chain, correctly extending the reversal one more node.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `reverseList` on [1,2,3,4,5] per the lesson's own step-by-step trace. After Step 3 (processing node 3), what is the state of `prev`, `curr`, and what does the partially-reversed chain look like?
options: prev=1, curr=3, chain still points forward

After Step 3: prev=3 (the last reversed node so far), curr=4 (the next to process) — the partially-reversed segment is 3->2->1->null, while 4->5->null remains forward; the lesson's trace confirms: 'Step 3: prev=2, curr=3, next=4: 3->2. prev=3, curr=4'
After Step 3 the entire list is already fully reversed
prev=5, curr=1 — reversal starts from the tail
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact step-by-step trace: at each step, the current node's next is redirected to prev (reversing one link), then both prev and curr advance — after Step 3, prev holds node 3 (the current reversed-chain head) and curr holds node 4 (the next node to reverse), with 3->2->1->null reversed and 4->5->null still intact.

logic_mcq.question: What is the final return value of `reverseList` for input [1,2,3,4,5], and why is `prev` returned rather than `curr`?
options: curr is returned because it's the last node processed

prev is returned because when the loop terminates (curr===null, meaning we've processed all nodes), `prev` is pointing to the LAST NODE we reversed — which is the original list's final node (5) and now the first node of the fully reversed list; returning curr would return null, which is useless
head is returned because the original head never changes
The function returns void; the caller must track the new head separately
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact statement: 'return prev; // prev is now the new head' — the loop terminates when curr reaches null (past the last node), at which point prev holds the last node we processed, which is the original tail node (5) and is now the head of the reversed list 5->4->3->2->1->null.

syntax_mcq.question: In `reverseBetween`, why is `prev.next.next = curr` executed BEFORE `prev.next = tail` when reconnecting the reversed sublist?
options: The order is arbitrary and doesn't matter

After the sublist reversal, `prev.next` still refers to the ORIGINAL left node (now the tail of the reversed sublist) — we need this reference to connect it to `curr` (the first node after the right boundary); if `prev.next = tail` were done first, we'd lose the reference to the original left node (now the sublist tail) before connecting it to `curr`, breaking the chain
Both lines perform the same operation and could be collapsed into one
prev.next is always null at this point, so order is irrelevant
syntax_mcq.explanation: Order is critical here: `prev.next` still points to the original left-boundary node (now the reversed sublist's tail), which needs to be connected to `curr` (the node after right) BEFORE `prev.next` is overwritten to point to `tail` (the new sublist head); doing it in reverse order would lose the reference to the original left node before the chain is properly reconnected.

lessons.title: Doubly Linked List
lessons.objective: Implement a doubly linked list with prev and next pointers, understand the O(1) delete-given-node capability, and see why it is the backing structure for LRU Cache and browser history.
concepts: Doubly linked list node: val, prev, next pointers
Sentinel head and tail: eliminate all boundary conditions
Insert between two nodes: O(1) with four pointer updates
Delete a given node directly: O(1) without predecessor traversal
Why DLL enables O(1) delete: prev pointer eliminates predecessor search
Doubly linked list vs singly: 2x pointer overhead, O(1) delete benefit
Browser history: forward and backward navigation
LRU Cache: O(1) move-to-front and O(1) remove-from-back
lessons.explanation: A doubly linked list adds a prev pointer to each node in addition to next. This single addition has a profound consequence: you can delete any node in O(1) without needing to find its predecessor first. In a singly linked list, deleting a node requires O(n) traversal to find the predecessor. With a prev pointer, the predecessor is at node.prev — O(1) access. Insert between two known nodes: given nodes A and C, insert B between them by setting B.next = C, B.prev = A, A.next = B, C.prev = B. Four pointer updates, O(1). Sentinel nodes (dummy head and dummy tail) eliminate all boundary conditions: the list is never empty (sentinels are always present), and insertions and deletions never need to check for null boundaries. This makes doubly linked list code dramatically cleaner than singly linked list code with boundary checking.
lessons.analogy: A doubly linked list is a two-lane road where every car has both a forward link (next car) and a backward link (previous car). To remove any car from the convoy, you just tell the car behind it to link forward to the car ahead of it, and vice versa. In a one-way road (singly linked list), you must drive from the front to find the car just before the one you want to remove before you can do anything.

code_example.explanation: The sentinel nodes eliminate every boundary check. Without sentinels, addToFront must check if the list is empty. Without sentinels, removeFromBack must check if the list has exactly one element. With sentinels, the real nodes are always between head.next and tail.prev, so insertBetween and remove work identically for any node including the first and last real nodes.

common_mistakes: Not updating all four pointers when inserting between two nodes — inserting B between A and C requires setting B.next, B.prev, A.next, and C.prev; missing any one of the four creates a broken chain

Not nullifying the removed node's prev and next after deletion — leaving removed.prev and removed.next pointing into the list creates memory leaks and potential use-after-delete bugs; set them to null after removal
Forgetting to check that the list is non-empty before removeFromBack even with sentinels — if size is 0, tail.prev is the dummy head, not a real node; removing the dummy head corrupts the list
lessons.interview_relevance: Doubly linked lists are rarely asked in isolation but are the implementation backbone of LRU Cache (Lesson 9), which is one of the most asked design problems in interviews. Interviewers specifically ask 'what data structure would you use for the cache eviction mechanism?' — the answer is a doubly linked list because it gives O(1) move-to-front and O(1) remove-from-back.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement DoublyLinkedList above with a moveToFront(node) method that moves any existing node to the front of the list in O(1). Test it by adding nodes [1,2,3,4,5], moving node 3 to the front, and verifying the list is [3,1,2,4,5]. State why moveToFront requires O(1) with a doubly linked list but O(n) with a singly linked list.

visual_explanation.description: Draw a doubly linked list with sentinels. Sentinel HEAD ⟷ node(A) ⟷ node(B) ⟷ node(C) ⟷ Sentinel TAIL. Show both prev (←) and next (→) arrows for each link. Highlight that HEAD.next=A and TAIL.prev=C, and A.prev=HEAD and C.next=TAIL. Then show node(B) deletion: B.prev.next=B.next (A.next=C), B.next.prev=B.prev (C.prev=A). Result: HEAD ⟷ A ⟷ C ⟷ TAIL. Node B is disconnected. Label 'O(1) deletion — no traversal needed because node.prev gives direct access to predecessor'. Compare: SLL would need to traverse from HEAD to A to find B's predecessor.

interview_war_story.story: The interviewer asked 'Design an LRU Cache. What data structure handles the eviction in O(1)?' The candidate said 'An array.' Interviewer: 'How would you move a recently used element to the front?' Candidate: 'Shift all elements right and insert at 0.' Interviewer: 'What is the complexity?' Candidate: 'O(n).' Interviewer: 'We need O(1).' Candidate after thinking: 'A doubly linked list. The node has a prev pointer so I can remove it in O(1) without traversal, then insert at front in O(1). A singly linked list cannot do this because removing a node requires its predecessor which I cannot get without O(n) traversal.' That answer was correct. The prev pointer is the entire reason for choosing DLL over SLL for LRU.
interview_war_story.lesson: The prev pointer in a doubly linked list converts O(n) node deletion to O(1). This single property is why DLL is used for LRU Cache. When an interviewer asks 'why doubly not singly?', the answer is: O(1) delete of any given node.

questions.question: Why can a doubly linked list delete any node in O(1), while a singly linked list requires O(n)?
options: Doubly linked lists are faster

In a singly linked list, deleting a node requires its predecessor to perform prev.next = node.next. Finding the predecessor takes O(n) traversal. In a doubly linked list, node.prev IS the predecessor — O(1) direct access.
Doubly linked lists have more memory
The algorithm is different
questions.explanation: Deletion requires: predecessor.next = node.next. In a singly linked list, predecessor requires O(n) traversal from head. In a doubly linked list, node.prev points directly to the predecessor — no traversal needed. The prev pointer is the key that converts O(n) to O(1) deletion.

questions.question: Sentinel head and tail nodes in a doubly linked list eliminate what edge cases?
options: They eliminate nothing — they are just empty nodes

They eliminate: (1) checking if the list is empty before insert/delete, (2) special-casing the first real node (no prev) and last real node (no next). All real nodes always have both prev and next pointing to valid nodes (possibly sentinels).
They speed up the algorithm
They are required for correctness
questions.explanation: Without sentinels: insertFront must check if list is empty. removeFromBack must check if list has exactly 1 element. With sentinels: head.next is always valid (either the first real node or the tail sentinel). Every real node always has prev and next. The same _insertBetween and _remove code works for all positions including first and last real nodes.

questions.question: A DLL node stores both key and val. Why must the node store the key?
options: For faster key lookup
When evicting the LRU node from the back of the DLL (tail.prev), you must also delete that key from the hash map. Without the key stored in the node, you cannot identify which map entry to delete.
For display purposes
The key is not needed in the node
questions.explanation: During eviction: you have the node reference (from tail.prev) but need to call map.delete(key). The map stores key→node. Going from node back to key requires the key to be in the node. This is the most commonly forgotten detail in LRU Cache implementation.

hints.text: _insertBetween: 4 pointer updates — node.prev=prevNode, node.next=nextNode, prevNode.next=node, nextNode.prev=node. All four are required. _remove: node.prev.next=node.next; node.next.prev=node.prev; then null out node's pointers.

moveToFront: _remove(node) removes from current position. Then _insertBetween(node, this.head, this.head.next) inserts right after the head sentinel. Since _remove decrements size and the caller of addToFront increments, track size carefully in moveToFront.
moveToFront: this._remove(node); this._insertBetween(node, this.head, this.head.next); this.size++; (because _remove did size-- and we need net 0 change)

theory_mcq.question: Why does a doubly linked list (DLL) enable O(1) deletion of ANY given node — including middle nodes — while a singly linked list requires O(n) for the same operation when only given the target node?
options: Doubly linked lists don't actually support O(1) deletion; they are identical to singly linked lists in this respect

A DLL node stores BOTH a `prev` pointer (to its predecessor) AND a `next` pointer (to its successor) — given any node, `node.prev.next = node.next` and `node.next.prev = node.prev` can directly bypass the node in O(1) using the stored prev reference; a singly linked list node only stores `next`, so there's no shortcut to the predecessor and an O(n) traversal from head is required to find it
O(1) deletion in a DLL requires the node to be the head or tail only
The O(1) cost comes from the sentinel nodes, not the prev pointer
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's core 'Why DLL enables O(1) delete' point: the `prev` pointer on every node is precisely the predecessor reference that makes O(1) deletion possible — with it, you can update both the predecessor's `next` AND the successor's `prev` in four O(1) pointer updates without any traversal.

theory_mcq.question: What is the purpose of SENTINEL head and tail nodes in the DoublyLinkedList implementation, and what edge cases do they eliminate?
options: Sentinel nodes are placeholder values stored at the first and last positions as actual data

Sentinel nodes are permanent dummy nodes that are NEVER removed and always bracket the real data — they eliminate all boundary-condition checks: `_insertBetween` and `_remove` never need to check 'is this the first/last real node?' because real nodes always have a genuine predecessor (the dummy head or another real node) AND a genuine successor (another real node or the dummy tail), making every operation's pointer logic identical regardless of position
Sentinel nodes improve cache performance by keeping memory contiguous
Sentinel nodes are only used when the list has exactly zero or one real element
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concept: 'Sentinel head and tail: eliminate all boundary conditions' — by guaranteeing that every real node always has both a prev (at minimum the dummy head) and a next (at minimum the dummy tail), the insert and remove operations can use uniform 4-pointer logic without special-casing empty lists, single-element lists, or head/tail operations.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the lesson's DoublyLinkedList demo: `addToFront(1); addToFront(2); addToFront(3);`. What does `toArray()` return, and why does addToFront(3) produce [3,2,1] rather than [1,2,3]?
options: [1,2,3] — addToFront appends to the back

[3,2,1] — each addToFront inserts AFTER the dummy head (the MRU/front position), so the most recently added value always ends up first: 1 is added first (list: [1]), then 2 is inserted before 1 (list: [2,1]), then 3 is inserted before 2 (list: [3,2,1]) — confirmed by the lesson's own console.log output
[3,1,2] — elements are inserted in random order
[1] — only the last addToFront takes effect
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's confirmed output: `console.log(dll.toArray()); // [3, 2, 1]` — each addToFront calls `_insertBetween(node, this.head, this.head.next)`, placing the new node immediately after the dummy head; the last-inserted node always ends up at the front, giving LIFO ordering in the output.

logic_mcq.question: After `addToFront(1); addToFront(2); addToFront(3); dll._remove(n2);`, what does `toArray()` return, and why can `_remove(n2)` be called directly without knowing n2's position?
options: [3,2,1] — _remove doesn't actually remove the node

[3,1] — _remove uses n2's own `prev` and `next` pointers to bypass it: `n2.prev.next = n2.next` (makes 3 skip over 2 to reach 1) and `n2.next.prev = n2.prev` (makes 1 look back to 3), all in O(1) without any traversal; the lesson confirms: `dll._remove(n2); // delete middle node directly — O(1)`
[2,1] — only the head changes during remove
The operation throws an error since n2's position is unknown
logic_mcq.explanation: This demonstrates the core DLL advantage: since n2 stores both `n2.prev` (node 3) and `n2.next` (node 1), the four pointer updates needed for removal are all O(1) — no traversal needed to find the predecessor since the prev pointer IS the predecessor, directly matching the lesson's output `console.log(dll.toArray()); // [3, 1]`.

syntax_mcq.question: In `_remove(node)`, why are `node.prev = null; node.next = null;` executed after the pointer updates, and what does the comment '// help GC' mean?
options: These lines reverse the previous pointer updates and are incorrect

After the two pointer updates (bypassing the node from both directions), the removed node is logically disconnected from the list but its `prev` and `next` still point INTO the list — nulling them out removes these references so the JavaScript garbage collector can reclaim the removed node's memory if no other variables hold a reference to it; 'GC' stands for Garbage Collector
These lines set the sentinel nodes' values to null
null assignments are required syntax after every pointer update in JavaScript
syntax_mcq.explanation: After the two bypassing pointer updates, the removed node is unreachable from the DLL's sentinel head/tail chain, but still references its old neighbors through its own prev/next — clearing these prevents the removed node from holding live references into the still-active list, helping the garbage collector identify and reclaim the node's memory.

lessons.title: Fast And Slow Pointer Pattern
lessons.objective: Apply the fast-and-slow pointer technique to find the middle of a linked list, detect cycles, and solve problems requiring simultaneous traversal at different speeds.
concepts: Fast pointer moves 2 steps, slow pointer moves 1 step per iteration
Find middle: when fast reaches end, slow is at middle
Odd vs even length: off-by-one distinction for middle
Palindrome linked list: find middle, reverse second half, compare
Reorder list: find middle, reverse second half, interleave
Cycle detection preview: fast catches slow inside a cycle
Why fast reaches end in n/2 iterations: proof
Two-pointer spacing for kth-from-end problems
lessons.explanation: The fast-and-slow pointer pattern uses two pointers on the same list advancing at different speeds. The slow pointer moves one node per step; the fast pointer moves two. When fast reaches the end of the list, slow is exactly at the middle. For an odd-length list of n nodes, slow stops at position n/2 (the exact middle). For even-length, it stops at n/2 (the first of the two middle nodes) or n/2+1 depending on whether the condition is fast.next or fast.next.next. The proof: fast covers n steps in the time slow covers n/2, so when fast has traversed the full list, slow has traversed half. This pattern generalises: any fixed speed ratio gives a fixed distance relationship between the two pointers when fast stops. For k-steps-behind: advance one pointer k steps, then advance both at equal speed until the lead pointer reaches the end. The trailing pointer is exactly k steps from the end.
lessons.analogy: Fast and slow pointers are two runners on a circular track. The fast runner moves at twice the speed of the slow runner. When the fast runner has completed one full lap, the slow runner has completed half a lap and is at the midpoint. For a non-circular track, when the fast runner reaches the finish line, the slow runner is exactly halfway. The predictable positional relationship between the two runners based on their speed ratio is what makes the pattern useful.

code_example.explanation: In reorderList, fast.next && fast.next.next (not just fast && fast.next) is used so that for even-length lists, slow stops at the first of the two middles, ensuring the first half is >= the second half in length. This prevents the interleaving from trying to access a null second-half node.

common_mistakes: Not cutting the list in half before reversing the second half in reorderList — without slow.next = null, the reversed second half still points back into the first half, creating a cycle during interleaving

Using fast && fast.next.next vs fast.next && fast.next.next — these give different middle positions for even-length lists; trace through [1,2,3,4] with both conditions to see which middle node each produces

Forgetting to restore the list after isPalindrome — the palindrome check reverses the second half in-place; if the problem requires the list to be unchanged after the check, you must reverse the second half back
lessons.interview_relevance: Linked List Cycle (#141), Middle of the Linked List (#876), Palindrome Linked List (#234), and Reorder List (#143) are all NeetCode 150 / Blind 75 problems that use fast-and-slow pointers. The pattern appears in virtually every second linked list interview problem. Being able to code findMiddle from memory and explain why slow stops at the middle is a baseline expectation.

Then solve Reorder List: implement reorderList and verify [1,2,3,4] becomes [1,4,2,3] and [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [1,5,2,4,3]. visual_explanation.description: Draw [1,2,3,4,5] with fast and slow both starting at node 1. Show 3 iterations: Iter 1: slow→2, fast→3. Iter 2: slow→3, fast→5. Iter 3: fast.next=null, loop exits. slow=node3 (middle). Below: show 3-step reorderList. Step 1: middle=node3, cut: 3.next=null. Now two independent lists: [1,2,3] and [4,5]. Step 2: reverse [4,5] → [5,4,null], prev=5. Step 3: interleave — draw one iteration: first=1, second=5. first.next=5, 5.next=2. Advance to first=2, second=4. Continue. Final: [1,5,2,4,3]. Annotate: 'The CUT (slow.next=null) is what makes the two halves independent during reversal and interleaving'.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Reorder List. The candidate correctly found the middle, reversed the second half, and interleaved. But they did not cut the list (forgot slow.next = null). Their code produced [1,4,2,3,2,3,4] for [1,2,3,4] — elements repeated. The interviewer asked them to trace the interleave step. The candidate traced: 'After interleaving first=3, second=4, tmp1=3.next which is... 4 (the original forward pointer from 3 to 4). The cut would have removed that.' The candidate added slow.next = null and it worked. The interviewer said: 'Linked list problems always need you to explicitly break old connections — they do not break themselves.'
interview_war_story.lesson: In linked list rearrangement, old pointer connections persist until you explicitly break them. slow.next=null cuts the first half from the second half. Without it, nodes in the first half still point into the second half, causing wrong or cyclic results during rearrangement.

questions.question: When fast reaches the end of a 5-node list, where is slow?
options: At the last node
At the first node
At the 3rd node — the middle. When fast takes n steps, slow takes n/2. For n=5 nodes, slow stops at position ceil(5/2)=3.
At the 2nd node
questions.explanation: Fast moves 2 steps per iteration, slow moves 1. When fast has moved n total steps (reaching the end), slow has moved n/2 steps. For 5 nodes, fast moves 4-5 steps while slow moves 2-3 steps, stopping at the middle (node 3, 1-indexed).

questions.question: In isPalindrome, you find the middle, reverse the second half, compare, then return. What should you do before returning true?
options: Nothing — return true
Reverse the second half back to restore the original list, if the problem requires the list to be unchanged
Delete the second half
This step is not needed
questions.explanation: isPalindrome reverses the second half in-place as a side effect of the algorithm. If the caller expects the list to remain unchanged (e.g., 'check without modifying the list'), you must restore it by reversing the second half again before returning. Many interview problems explicitly say 'do not modify the input' — check whether that constraint applies.

questions.question: In reorderList on [1,2,3,4,5], after finding the middle (node 3), you set slow.next = null. Why?
options: Saves memory

Cutting the list at the middle creates two independent lists: [1,2,3] and [4,5]. Without this cut, when you reverse [4,5,null], the next pointer from 3 would still point into the reversed second half, creating a cycle during interleaving.
Required by JavaScript
It is not necessary
questions.explanation: Without slow.next = null, the original node 3's next pointer still points to node 4 after reversing. When you interleave and eventually reach node 3 in the first half, its next pointer leads back into the already-rearranged second half, creating wrong ordering or a cycle. Cutting the list makes the two halves completely independent.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Forgetting slow.next = null before reversing the second half. Without this cut, node 3 still points to node 4 after the reversal. During interleaving, the first half eventually reaches node 3 whose next pointer leads into the reversed second half out of order.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n) time but wrong output — list not properly split before reversal

Critical: slow.next=null before the reversal loop. This cuts the list into two independent halves. Without it, after reversing the second half, the original middle node still points into it, creating wrong connections during interleave.
Interleave: const tmp1=first.next,tmp2=second.next; first.next=second; second.next=tmp1; first=tmp1; second=tmp2;

theory_mcq.question: Why does the fast pointer (moving 2 steps per iteration) cause `slow` to stop at the middle after n/2 iterations, and what is the loop condition `while (fast && fast.next)` specifically guarding against?
options: The fast pointer always reaches the middle, not the end

Since fast moves 2 steps per iteration and slow moves 1, fast covers the list twice as quickly — after n/2 iterations, fast has covered n steps (reached the end) while slow has covered n/2 steps (the middle); the condition `fast && fast.next` guards against NULL POINTER errors: `fast` checks fast hasn't fallen off the list (odd-length final step), and `fast.next` checks there's a valid second step (preventing null.next access on even-length lists' final iteration)
The loop condition is incorrect and the algorithm requires a separate length calculation
fast moves 1 step and slow moves 2 steps; the question has them reversed
theory_mcq.explanation: The n/2 convergence follows from the 2:1 speed ratio — when fast exhausts the list (n steps), slow has taken n/2 steps, landing at the middle; the two-part condition `fast && fast.next` handles both even-length lists (fast lands on the last node, fast.next===null, stopping before an invalid double-step) and odd-length lists (fast lands on null, stopping cleanly).

theory_mcq.question: For a 4-node list [1,2,3,4], `findMiddle` returns the node with value 3 (the SECOND of two middle nodes), not 2 (the first). Why does this occur with the given loop condition?
options: findMiddle([1,2,3,4]) actually returns 2 per the lesson's stated comment

For a 4-node list, the loop executes TWICE before `fast.next` becomes null: after step 1, slow=2 and fast=3; after step 2, slow=3 and fast=null (fast advanced to node 4 then to null via fast.next.next); the loop then exits with slow=3 — this was confirmed by independent step-by-step execution tracing, which reveals the lesson's own comment claiming 'slow stops at 2 (first of two middles)' for a 4-node list is actually incorrect for this implementation
findMiddle is non-deterministic and returns different nodes each run
The loop always returns the first node regardless of list length
theory_mcq.explanation: This is a verified source-file discrepancy: the lesson's comment claims 'slow stops at 2 (first of two middles)' for [1,2,3,4], but direct step-by-step execution traces `slow` landing at node 3 (the second middle) — step 1: slow=2, fast=3; step 2: slow=3, fast=null. The code correctly implements a valid 'upper middle' strategy, but the comment misidentifies which of the two middles is returned.

logic_mcq.question: In `isPalindrome([1,2,2,1])`, after finding the middle and reversing the second half, what are the two sub-lists being compared left-to-right, and why does this confirm the list is a palindrome?
options: The entire list is compared against itself, which always returns true

After findMiddle, slow=2 (index 2 for a 4-node list, per verified behavior); reversing from slow gives the second half as 1->2->null; comparing left (starting from the original head, 1->2->2->1) against right (the reversed second half, 1->2->null) — the right pointer exhausts after matching 1==1 and 2==2, confirming palindrome; the right side is shorter and drives the loop termination
The comparison always returns false for even-length lists
Only the first and last nodes are compared; middle nodes are ignored
logic_mcq.explanation: For [1,2,2,1] with the 4-node findMiddle returning the second middle node (index 2, value 2): reversing from that node produces 1->2->null as the reversed second half; comparing left (1->2->...) against right (1->2->null) matches both values before right exhausts, returning true — the while(right) loop drives termination, so only as many comparisons as right-side nodes are made.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `reorderList` use `while (fast.next && fast.next.next)` for its middle-finding (with `fast` starting at `head.next`) rather than the standard `while (fast && fast.next)` used in `findMiddle`?
options: Both loop conditions produce identical results; the choice is purely stylistic

reorderList needs to split the list into two halves at `slow` (cutting with `slow.next = null`), and uses a slightly different stopping condition to ensure the split yields a LEFT half that's length <= RIGHT half for even-length inputs — the `fast = head.next` start with `fast.next && fast.next.next` is tuned to stop slow one node EARLIER, giving the left half at most one extra node versus the right half, which is the correct split point for interleaving
The different condition is required to prevent an infinite loop
fast.next and fast.next.next are always identical expressions
logic_mcq.explanation: The findMiddle and sortList/reorderList middle-finding variants differ subtly in their stopping conditions to achieve different split behaviors — reorderList intentionally stops slow one position earlier (the last node of the first half vs. the first node of the second half) to ensure the cut `slow.next = null` cleanly separates the two halves for interleaving, versus findMiddle's goal of identifying the mid-node itself.

syntax_mcq.question: In `reorderList`, `slow.next = null` is executed AFTER finding the middle and BEFORE reversing the second half. What would happen if this cut were omitted?
options: Nothing changes; slow.next = null is unnecessary

Without cutting the list at `slow.next = null`, the first half would still be linked to the second half — when `sortList` or `reorderList` then reverses the second half starting from `slow.next`, the reversal would also follow the original next pointers into the first half, creating a cycle or corrupting the first half of the list; the null cut ensures the two halves are completely independent before manipulation begins
slow.next = null deletes the node at the middle
The cut causes both halves to become null
syntax_mcq.explanation: The null cut is essential for separation: without it, the second half's reversal loop would follow original next pointers that still link back into the first half, causing undefined/corrupted behavior (potentially reversing more than intended or creating a cycle); cutting at `slow.next = null` makes the first half a properly null-terminated list independent of the second half.
