lessons.title: Detect Cycle — Floyd's Algorithm
lessons.objective: Implement Floyd's cycle detection algorithm to detect and find the start of a cycle in O(n) time and O(1) space, and prove why the two pointers must meet inside the cycle.
concepts: Cycle definition: a node's next pointer points to an earlier node
Naive detection: hash set of visited nodes — O(n) space
Floyd's algorithm: fast and slow pointers meet inside cycle
Proof: relative speed of 1 step/iteration means fast catches slow
Phase 1: detect meeting point inside cycle
Phase 2: find cycle start using distance arithmetic
Phase 2 proof: distance from head to cycle start equals distance from meeting point to cycle start
Find cycle length: count steps from meeting point back to itself
lessons.explanation: A cycle in a linked list occurs when a node's next pointer points to a previously visited node, creating an infinite loop. Naive detection: use a Set to track visited nodes. O(n) time and O(n) space. Floyd's algorithm achieves O(1) space. Phase 1: start slow and fast at head. Move slow one step and fast two steps per iteration. If they meet, a cycle exists. Why they must meet: inside the cycle, fast gains one step on slow per iteration. If the cycle has length C, fast will catch slow within C iterations of both entering the cycle. Phase 2: find the cycle start. After meeting, reset one pointer to head. Move both pointers one step at a time. They meet at the cycle start. The mathematical proof relies on: if the cycle starts at distance F from head, and the meeting point is at distance C-k from the cycle start (where k varies), then F = C-k, meaning the head pointer and the meeting-point pointer arrive at the cycle start simultaneously.
lessons.analogy: Floyd's algorithm is two runners on a track where part of the track is a loop. The faster runner will always lap the slower runner inside the loop — they are guaranteed to meet somewhere on the circular portion. After meeting, one runner returns to the start line and both run at the same speed. By the mathematical relationship between the track distances, they arrive at the loop entrance (cycle start) at exactly the same time.

code_example.explanation: The Phase 2 proof is the most important mathematical argument in this module. The key insight: F = n*C - k means the distance from head to cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to cycle start (going forward around the cycle). This is why resetting slow to head and advancing both at speed 1 makes them meet at the cycle start.

common_mistakes: Checking slow === fast before moving the pointers — at initialisation both pointers are at head, so they are trivially equal; check for equality AFTER moving both pointers each iteration

Using slow === fast to check equality instead of comparing node references — in JavaScript, === on objects compares references, which is correct here; using == also works for objects but === is safer and more explicit
Not handling the no-cycle case in detectCycle before Phase 2 — if the while loop exits because fast or fast.next is null (no cycle), proceeding to Phase 2 will cause a null pointer error
lessons.interview_relevance: Linked List Cycle (#141) and Linked List Cycle II (#142, find cycle start) are both Blind 75 / NeetCode 150. Floyd's algorithm is one of the algorithms interviewers most frequently ask you to prove in addition to implement. Being able to state 'relative speed of 1 step/iteration means fast catches slow within C iterations' and sketch the Phase 2 distance proof demonstrates mathematical maturity.
lessons.mini_challenge: Create a linked list [3,2,0,-4] where the tail's next pointer points to node at index 1 (value 2). Call detectCycle and verify it returns the node with value 2. Then answer these two questions in writing: (1) Why can't you use a hash set containing node indices instead of node references for cycle detection? (2) In Phase 2, if the cycle starts at the very head of the list (F=0), what happens? Does the algorithm still work correctly? Trace through the proof.

visual_explanation.description: Draw a linked list [3,2,0,-4] with nm4.next pointing back to n2 (forming a cycle). Show Phase 1: slow and fast both start at n3. Trace 3 iterations showing slow and fast positions. They meet inside the cycle (at n0 or nm4 depending on iteration count). Label this the MEETING POINT. Show Phase 2: reset slow to n3 (head). Both advance at speed 1. Draw arrows showing each step until they converge at n2 (cycle start). Label 'F=1 step from head to n2, also 1 step from meeting point to n2 (modulo cycle). They arrive simultaneously.' Below: write the proof summary: F+k=n×C, F=n×C-k.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Linked List Cycle II (find cycle start). The candidate implemented Phase 1 correctly but in Phase 2 continued moving fast at speed 2. 'I keep both at the same speed in Phase 2.' Interviewer: 'Fast is still moving 2 steps?' Candidate: 'Yes.' They traced: slow started at head, fast stayed at meeting point. Fast moved 2 per step, slow 1 per step. They never converged. Interviewer: 'Why 1 step?' Candidate thought about the proof: 'F = n×C - k. Slow needs exactly F steps from head to reach cycle start. Fast needs exactly F steps from meeting point. If fast moves 2 per step it would be at 2F steps past meeting point, not F.' Candidate fixed it to both speed 1 and it worked.
interview_war_story.lesson: Phase 2 of Floyd's algorithm requires BOTH pointers to move at speed 1. Fast must slow down. The proof relies on equal travel distances from head and meeting point to cycle start — doubling fast's speed breaks this symmetry.

questions.question: In Floyd's Phase 1, why must you check slow === fast AFTER moving both pointers, not before?
options: Order does not matter

At initialisation, both slow and fast are at head — they are trivially equal. Checking before moving would immediately return true (false positive) even for a list with no cycle. Check only AFTER moving.
The algorithm requires post-check
For performance
questions.explanation: At the start of every iteration, slow and fast could both be at the same node (especially at initialisation when both start at head). Checking before moving would trigger on the first iteration even with no cycle. The check must happen AFTER both pointers advance — that is the only meaningful equality test.

questions.question: After finding the meeting point in Phase 1, why do you reset slow to head and advance both at speed 1?
options: Arbitrary convention

The mathematical proof shows that the distance from head to cycle start (F) equals the distance from meeting point to cycle start (modulo cycle length). So starting one pointer at head and one at the meeting point, both at speed 1, guarantees they meet exactly at the cycle start.
To restart the algorithm
To find the cycle length instead
questions.explanation: Phase 2 uses the proof: F = n×C - k where F is distance head→cycle_start, C is cycle length, k is distance cycle_start→meeting_point. Resetting slow to head: slow travels F to cycle_start. Fast from meeting point travels n×C-k = F steps around the cycle, also landing at cycle_start. They meet there.

options: Nothing — Phase 2 handles both cases
If fast or fast.next is null after the loop, there is NO cycle — return null immediately. Without this check, Phase 2 would try to advance null pointers and throw an error.
Check if slow === null
Check list length
questions.explanation: The while loop exits in two cases: (1) cycle found — slow === fast inside the loop via break, or (2) no cycle — fast or fast.next is null. After the loop you must distinguish these. If fast is null or fast.next is null: no cycle, return null. Otherwise: cycle found, proceed to Phase 2.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Checking slow===fast BEFORE moving both pointers. At initialisation both are at head — trivially equal — returns true even with no cycle.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(1) but always returns true — equality check before any movement

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space — both phases.

hints.text: detectCycle Phase 2: after break, check if(!fast||!fast.next)return null (no cycle case). Then slow=head. While slow!==fast: slow=slow.next; fast=fast.next (speed 1). When they meet, that is the cycle start.
cycleLength: after detecting meeting point (slow===fast), start counting from slow.next back to slow. let len=1,curr=slow.next; while(curr!==slow){len++;curr=curr.next;} return len.
detectCycle Phase 2: if(!fast||!fast.next)return null; slow=head; while(slow!==fast){slow=slow.next;fast=fast.next;} return slow;

theory_mcq.question: In Floyd's cycle detection, why is it GUARANTEED that slow and fast will eventually meet inside the cycle (and not just skip past each other)?
options: They are not guaranteed to meet; sometimes they miss each other

Once both pointers are inside the cycle, the RELATIVE speed of fast with respect to slow is exactly 1 step per iteration (fast gains 1 node on slow each step since fast takes 2 steps and slow takes 1) — this means, from slow's perspective, fast is 'closing the gap' by exactly 1 each iteration; since the cycle is finite in length, fast will always CATCH slow after at most C iterations (where C is the cycle length), never skipping over it since the gap decreases by exactly 1 at each step
Meeting is only guaranteed when the cycle starts at the head node
They meet because JavaScript uses reference equality, not value equality
theory_mcq.explanation: The proof hinges on relative speed: once both pointers enter the cycle, fast gains exactly 1 position on slow per iteration (2 steps minus 1 step = net 1 step gain); the 'gap' between them reduces by 1 each step, and since it reduces by exactly 1 (not by 2 or more), it hits every integer value on the way to zero, guaranteeing a meeting rather than a skip.

theory_mcq.question: What does Phase 2 of Floyd's algorithm accomplish, and why does resetting one pointer to head (with both moving 1 step at a time) find the cycle START?
options: Phase 2 simply counts the total number of nodes in the cycle

Phase 2 exploits the mathematical relationship F = n*C - k (proven in the lesson), where F is the distance from head to cycle start, C is cycle length, k is the distance from cycle start to the meeting point, and n is some integer — after resetting slow to head and having both move 1 step at a time, slow travels F steps from head while fast travels F steps from the meeting point; F steps from the meeting point equals exactly (n*C - k) steps forward in the cycle, which arrives at the cycle start node — both arrive together
Phase 2 is only needed to count the cycle's length, not to find its start
Phase 2 works by reversing the cycle direction and re-running Phase 1
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's own proof: 'After reset: slow travels F from head, fast travels F from meeting point. fast travels F = n*C - k from meeting point, which is (n*C - k + k) = n*C steps around the cycle from cycle start = 0 steps past cycle start. Both arrive at cycle start simultaneously' — this elegant arithmetic equivalence is the core insight of Floyd's Phase 2.

logic_mcq.question: What is the difference between `hasCycle` and `detectCycle`, and when would you use each?
options: hasCycle and detectCycle are identical functions with different names

hasCycle (Phase 1 only) simply returns true/false indicating whether any cycle exists — O(1) space, used when only presence matters; detectCycle (Phase 1 + Phase 2) additionally finds and returns the EXACT NODE where the cycle begins — still O(1) space but more information, used when the cycle start position needs to be identified (e.g., LeetCode #142 Linked List Cycle II)
hasCycle returns the cycle start node; detectCycle only returns true/false
detectCycle uses O(n) space while hasCycle uses O(1)
logic_mcq.explanation: Both use O(1) space (no hash set), but hasCycle stops after Phase 1 (confirming a cycle exists) while detectCycle runs Phase 2 after Phase 1 to pinpoint the exact node where the cycle begins — the lesson maps these directly to LeetCode #141 (hasCycle) and #142 (detectCycle).

logic_mcq.question: In `detectCycle`, after Phase 1 finds the meeting point, why does Phase 2 move both pointers ONE step at a time (rather than keeping fast at 2 steps) when searching for the cycle start?
options: Phase 2 could use any step sizes; 1-step is just arbitrary convention

Phase 2 exploits the specific mathematical distance relationship F = n*C - k — this relationship guarantees that if both slow (from head) and fast (from meeting point) advance at EQUAL speeds (1 step each), they will meet exactly at the cycle start node after F steps; using different step sizes would break the arithmetic alignment that makes both pointers arrive at the same node simultaneously
Using 2 steps in Phase 2 would cause an infinite loop
Phase 2 uses 2 steps for fast; the question is incorrect
logic_mcq.explanation: The Phase 2 math only works when both pointers advance at the SAME rate — the F = n*C - k relationship shows that slow travels F from head while fast travels F from the meeting point, with equal speed ensuring both arrive at cycle start simultaneously; a different speed ratio would produce a different meeting point (not guaranteed to be the cycle start).

syntax_mcq.question: In `detectCycle`, after the Phase 1 loop breaks with `if (slow === fast) break;`, what does `if (!fast || !fast.next) return null;` check and why is it necessary?
options: This check always evaluates to false and is dead code

The Phase 1 loop can EXIT in two ways: either the break fires (meeting found, cycle detected) OR the while condition `fast && fast.next` becomes false naturally (fast reached the end, no cycle) — after the loop, we must distinguish which exit path occurred; if fast is null or fast.next is null, the loop exited because fast reached the end (no cycle), and we correctly return null; only if both fast and fast.next are non-null did a genuine meeting occur
This check verifies that the cycle is longer than 2 nodes
fast is guaranteed to be non-null after the loop; this check is unnecessary
syntax_mcq.explanation: The while-loop has two exit conditions: natural exit (fast or fast.next became null = no cycle) or break (slow===fast = cycle found) — after the loop, we can't know which happened without this explicit check; if fast or fast.next is null, it was a natural exit and we must return null rather than proceeding incorrectly to Phase 2.

lessons.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
lessons.objective: Merge two sorted linked lists in O(n+m) with O(1) space using the dummy head pattern, and extend it to merge k sorted lists efficiently.
concepts: Merge two sorted lists: compare heads, take smaller, advance
Dummy head: eliminates the 'which list is the new head?' question
O(n+m) time, O(1) space for two-list merge
Append remaining elements: one list may exhaust before the other
Merge k sorted lists: naive O(kN) vs heap O(N log k)
Divide-and-conquer merge: O(N log k) using merge sort structure
Sort a linked list: use merge sort, O(n log n) time O(log n) space
Connection to merge sort from Module 5
lessons.explanation: Merging two sorted linked lists is the linked list version of the merge step in merge sort. The approach: use a dummy head to avoid the question of which list's first node becomes the new head. Maintain a curr pointer starting at the dummy. At each step, compare list1.val and list2.val, attach the smaller to curr.next, and advance that list's pointer and curr. When one list is exhausted, attach the remainder of the other directly (no copying needed since it is already sorted). Total comparisons: O(n+m). Space: O(1) since we reuse existing nodes. Merge k sorted lists efficiently: a naive approach compares k heads at every step — O(kN) for N total nodes. Using a min-heap of size k that always holds the current smallest head of each list gives O(log k) per extraction, total O(N log k). The divide-and-conquer approach pairs lists and merges them, then pairs the results and merges again — same O(N log k) but without a heap.
lessons.analogy: Merging two sorted lists is like merging two sorted decks of cards face-up. Look at the top card of each deck, take whichever is smaller and add it to your merged pile. Repeat. When one deck runs out, add all remaining cards from the other deck directly — no need to look at them since they are already sorted and larger than everything in your merged pile.

code_example.explanation: In sortList, fast starts at head.next (not head). This ensures that for a two-node list [1,2], slow stops at node 1 (not node 2), so the split is [1] and [2]. If fast started at head, for [1,2] slow would advance once to node 2, and the cut would be null and [1,2], creating infinite recursion. The fast = head.next initialisation is a subtle but critical detail.

common_mistakes: Not using a dummy head and instead trying to determine the new head before the loop — the dummy head makes the first node comparison identical to all other comparisons; without it you need a special case to initialise the merged list head

Forgetting curr.next = list1 || list2 at the end — when one list is exhausted, the remaining nodes of the other list must be attached; without this, the merged list is truncated at the point where one list ran out

Initialising fast = head instead of fast = head.next in sortList — for two-element lists, fast = head causes slow to advance past the first node, making the first half empty and causing infinite recursion
lessons.interview_relevance: Merge Two Sorted Lists (#21) is Blind 75. Sort List (#148) is NeetCode 150. Merge K Sorted Lists (#23) is Blind 75 and one of the hardest Blind 75 problems. All three use the same mergeTwoLists function — learning it once unlocks three Blind 75 problems. The O(N log k) divide-and-conquer proof for merge k lists is specifically asked at Google and Amazon.

Finally, solve Merge K Sorted Lists using the divide-and-conquer approach on [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]] and verify the result is [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6].

visual_explanation.description: Draw the divide-and-conquer tree for merge k=4 sorted lists [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6],[0,2]]. Level 0: 4 lists. Level 1: merge([1,4,5],[1,3,4])=[1,1,3,4,4,5] and merge([2,6],[0,2])=[0,2,2,6]. Level 2: merge those two results=[0,1,1,2,2,3,4,4,5,6]. Label: log k=2 levels, O(N) merge work per level, total O(N log k). Contrast with naive approach (merge sequentially): [1,4,5]+[1,3,4]=[...], then +[2,6], then +[0,2] = 3 merges with growing lists = O(k×N) total.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Merge K Sorted Lists. The candidate said 'min-heap of size k' — correct. They coded it. The interviewer asked 'What is the time complexity?' Candidate: 'O(N log k) — each of N nodes is pushed and popped from a size-k heap, each operation O(log k).' Interviewer: 'Is there a way without a heap?' Candidate: 'Divide and conquer — merge pairs of lists, then pairs of results. Like merge sort. Same O(N log k) but log k levels of O(N) total merges instead.' Interviewer: 'Same complexity, why might you prefer one over the other?' Candidate: 'Divide and conquer avoids heap memory (O(k) space for heap vs O(1) extra for merge). Divide and conquer is also simpler to implement correctly.' That was the expected senior-level answer.
interview_war_story.lesson: When asked about merge k sorted lists, know both approaches: min-heap O(N log k) with O(k) space, and divide-and-conquer O(N log k) with O(1) extra space plus O(log k) call stack. The divide-and-conquer connection to merge sort is the deeper insight interviewers probe.

questions.question: In mergeTwoLists, why use a dummy head instead of tracking the new head separately?
options: Dummy head is faster

Without a dummy, you must separately determine which of list1.val or list2.val is smaller to initialise the merged list head, then handle all subsequent comparisons. With a dummy, the first comparison is identical to all others — no special initialisation needed.
Dummy head saves memory
The algorithm only works with a dummy
questions.explanation: Without dummy: you need code like 'let head = list1.val <= list2.val ? list1 : list2' before the loop, plus advancing that list. With dummy: curr = dummy. Every comparison, including the very first, is handled by the same loop body — attach smaller to curr.next, advance that list and curr. Uniform logic, no special cases.

questions.question: In sortList, fast starts at head.next (not head). Why?
options: To skip the first element

For a 2-node list [1,2]: if fast=head, the loop runs once (fast.next.next=null stops it), slow advances to node 2. cut: slow.next=null removes node 2 leaving only [1]. The right half is empty — infinite recursion. fast=head.next ensures slow stops at node 1, giving split [1] and [2].
Performance optimisation
head.next is always safer
questions.explanation: For [1,2] with fast=head: loop condition fast.next && fast.next.next. fast=node1, fast.next=node2, fast.next.next=null — condition false immediately. slow=head=node1. cut: slow.next=null. First half: [1], second half: null. sortList(null) returns null, infinite recursion risk avoided. But actually slow never advanced — so cut leaves first half as [1] and second half as starting from slow.next=null. The right sortList(null) returns null, then merge([1],null) returns [1]... actually it works. BUT for fast=head: 2-node list, slow doesn't advance = no split. Fast=head.next ensures an unambiguous split.

questions.question: Merge K sorted lists with divide-and-conquer has O(N log k) complexity. Why O(log k) and not O(k)?
options: Binary search is used

At each recursion level, pairs of lists are merged. Starting with k lists: level 1 gives k/2 merged lists, level 2 gives k/4, etc. There are log k levels. At each level the total work is O(N) (N total nodes merged). Total: O(N log k).
The heap has log k levels
k lists are sorted before merging
questions.explanation: The divide-and-conquer tree has log k levels (halving k lists at each level). At each level, the total number of nodes merged across all merges is N (each node is merged exactly once per level). Total: O(N) × O(log k) levels = O(N log k).

Why fast=head.next: for [1,2], fast=head.next=node2. Loop: fast.next=null → exits. slow=head=node1. mid=node2. Cut: node1.next=null. Left=sortList([1])=[1]. Right=sortList([2])=[2]. merge=[1,2]. Correct split.

theory_mcq.question: Why does `mergeTwoLists` use a dummy head node, and what specific problem does it solve compared to tracking the result head directly?
options: The dummy head is required by JavaScript syntax for linked list operations

Without a dummy head, deciding which list's node becomes the NEW result head requires an extra if-else before the loop — `mergeTwoLists` would need to initialize `resultHead` to whichever list's first element is smaller, which is a special case; with a dummy head, `curr` always has a predecessor to attach to (`curr.next = list1` or `curr.next = list2`), making the first iteration IDENTICAL to all subsequent iterations and eliminating the initialization special case entirely
The dummy head makes the algorithm O(1) space instead of O(n)
Dummy heads are only needed when merging exactly two lists, not k lists
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concept: 'Dummy head: eliminates the which list is the new head? question' — by having curr start at a throw-away dummy node, every attachment is uniform (`curr.next = smaller_node`); `return dummy.next` then strips the dummy, returning the real merged list head without any first-iteration special case.

theory_mcq.question: Why is `curr.next = list1 || list2` a correct one-liner for attaching remaining elements, rather than requiring a loop to copy them node-by-node?
options: This line only works when both lists are empty at this point

Since both list1 and list2 were ALREADY SORTED before the merge began, whichever list still has remaining elements after the main loop ends is GUARANTEED to be sorted and all greater than everything already in the result — attaching the remainder directly (as a contiguous sub-chain) in O(1) is safe and correct; no copying or re-sorting is needed, just a single pointer update to attach the remaining sorted tail
list1 || list2 merges both lists simultaneously in one operation
This is incorrect; a loop is always required to attach remaining elements
theory_mcq.explanation: Pre-sorted lists guarantee that any remaining elements are already in correct relative order and all larger than the last element placed in the result — so the remaining chain can be attached directly as-is in O(1), without iterating through it, since it's already correctly sorted for the merged result's tail.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `mergeTwoLists([1,2,4], [1,3,4])` step by step. Which node is taken at each of the first three comparisons, and what does the merged result look like?
options: The result is [1,1,2,3,4,4] — merge takes the smaller (or equal-and-left) node at each step
[1,2,4,1,3,4] — lists are simply concatenated
[1,3,4,1,2,4] — the second list always takes priority
The function throws an error when both lists have the same value at any position
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: step 1: list1.val=1 <= list2.val=1, take list1's 1 (advance list1); step 2: list1.val=2 > list2.val=1, take list2's 1 (advance list2); step 3: list1.val=2 <= list2.val=3, take list1's 2; continuing produces [1,1,2,3,4,4] — the `<=` comparison correctly takes from list1 when values are equal (stability).

logic_mcq.question: How does `mergeKLists` achieve O(N log k) using divide-and-conquer, rather than the naive O(kN) approach of merging one list at a time?
options: mergeKLists doesn't actually use divide-and-conquer; it merges lists sequentially

Like merge sort, `mergeKLists` recursively divides the k lists in half, merges each half independently, then merges the two resulting lists — at each LEVEL of the recursion tree, the total work is O(N) (merging the same N total nodes, just across different pairs); since the tree has O(log k) levels (halving k lists each time), total work is O(N log k) vs naive's O(kN) where k merge passes each scan all N nodes
O(N log k) is only achieved when k equals exactly log N
mergeKLists uses a hash map to avoid redundant comparisons
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit analysis: 'At each level: total nodes N, O(N) merge work. log k levels (halving k lists each level). Total: O(N log k)' — the same recursion-tree argument used for merge sort in L1-M05, applied to k lists instead of n elements.

syntax_mcq.question: In `sortList`, why does `fast` start at `head.next` (not `head`) for the middle-finding step, compared to `findMiddle` which starts `fast` at `head`?
options: This is a copy-paste error; both should start fast at head

Starting `fast` at `head.next` (with the `fast.next && fast.next.next` stopping condition) causes `slow` to stop one position EARLIER — for a 4-node list, `slow` lands on node 2 (the first middle) rather than node 3, giving a more even split when `slow.next = null` cuts the list into two halves for recursive sorting; this balanced cut improves performance in practice by minimizing the length imbalance between the two halves
head.next is used to skip the dummy head node
fast starting at head.next makes the algorithm O(n) instead of O(n log n)
syntax_mcq.explanation: The `fast = head.next` + `fast.next && fast.next.next` variant produces a different (earlier) stopping point for `slow` compared to the standard `fast = head` + `fast && fast.next`, achieving a more balanced split especially for even-length lists — the lesson intentionally uses this variant for `sortList` to ensure the two halves have as equal length as possible before recursive sorting.

lessons.title: Remove Nth Node From End
lessons.objective: Remove the nth node from the end of a linked list in one pass using the two-pointer spacing technique.
concepts: One-pass constraint: single traversal, O(n)
Two-pointer spacing: advance lead n+1 steps, then move both
When lead reaches null, trail is at predecessor of target
Dummy head: handles removal of actual head (n = list length)
Off-by-one: advance n+1 steps (not n) to land on predecessor
Why n+1 not n: trail must be at predecessor, not at target
Generalisation: kth from end using same spacing pattern
Connection to fast-and-slow: fixed distance between pointers
lessons.explanation: Remove the nth node from the end of a linked list in one pass. Two-pointer spacing: start both pointers at a dummy node placed before head. Advance the lead pointer n+1 steps. Now lead is n+1 nodes ahead of trail. Advance both pointers one step at a time until lead is null (one step past the last node). At this point, trail is exactly at the predecessor of the nth node from the end. Set trail.next = trail.next.next to remove it. Why n+1 steps instead of n: if we advance lead only n steps, when lead reaches the last node, trail is at the nth node itself (not its predecessor). We cannot delete a node without its predecessor in a singly linked list. Advancing one extra step ensures trail stops one before the target. The dummy head handles the case n = list length (removing the actual head): trail stays at the dummy, and trail.next = trail.next.next removes the head correctly.
lessons.analogy: Two-pointer spacing is like two hikers walking a trail where one starts n+1 steps ahead of the other. When the lead hiker reaches the end of the trail, the trailing hiker is exactly n+1 steps from the end, which puts them one step before the target node. They both walk at the same pace after the initial offset is established.

code_example.explanation: The loop condition i <= n gives exactly n+1 iterations (i=0,1,...,n). This is equivalent to a two-phase approach: advance lead n steps to be n nodes ahead, then advance one more step to create the n+1 gap. Using i <= n is more concise than i < n+1 but produces the same result.

common_mistakes: Advancing lead n steps instead of n+1 — n steps puts trail at the target node (not the predecessor); deletion requires the predecessor; always advance n+1 steps from the dummy node

Not using a dummy head — without a dummy, removing the actual head (when n equals the list length) requires a special case; with a dummy, trail sits at the dummy when removing the head, and the deletion formula works identically

Using lead != null check instead of advancing exactly n+1 steps — the number of advance steps must be exactly n+1; a while loop without a counter may advance the wrong number of steps; use a for loop with a counter
lessons.interview_relevance: Remove Nth Node From End (#19) is Blind 75. It is a standard medium problem used to test two-pointer spacing and dummy head pattern knowledge. Solving it in a naive two-pass approach (find length, then remove) gets credit but demonstrates less fluency with the linked list toolkit.

Step 1: advance lead 3 times (n+1=3): after step1 lead=1, step2 lead=2, step3 lead=3. Trail still at dummy. Now advance both until lead=null: both advance→lead=4,trail=1; both advance→lead=5,trail=2; both advance→lead=null,trail=3. Trail at node3 (predecessor of node4). trail.next=trail.next.next: 3.next=5. Result [1,2,3,5]. Label: 'SPACING = n+1 = 3. When lead=null, trail is exactly at the predecessor of the nth-from-end node.' Below: show what goes wrong with n steps — trail at node4 (the target), cannot delete itself.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Remove Nth Node From End. The candidate advanced lead n steps (not n+1). Their code removed the wrong node: for [1,2,3,4,5] n=2, they removed node 5 instead of node 4. The interviewer said 'What node should be removed?' Candidate: '4 — the 2nd from end.' Interviewer: 'Where is trail when lead reaches node5 (the last node)?' The candidate traced: after 2 steps from dummy, lead=node2 and trail=dummy. After advancing both until lead=node5: lead=5, trail=3. But I need trail to be at 3 to delete 4. That is correct — trail IS at 3. Candidate looked again: 'Oh, n=2 steps from dummy puts lead at node2, not node3. I need n+1=3 steps to put lead at node3, so when lead=null, trail=3.' Fixed in 30 seconds.
interview_war_story.lesson: n steps puts lead at node-n. When lead reaches the last real node, trail is n behind = at the nth-from-end node itself. n+1 steps puts lead at node-n+1. When lead=null, trail is n+1 behind = one before the nth-from-end = the predecessor. Always use n+1.

questions.question: You advance the lead pointer n+1 steps (not n) from the dummy node. Why n+1?
options: Off-by-one error in the algorithm

After n+1 steps, lead is n+1 ahead of trail (both starting at dummy). When lead reaches null (n+1 past the last node), trail is at the predecessor of the nth-from-end node — exactly where you need it to perform trail.next = trail.next.next.
n steps puts trail at the target node
n+1 is arbitrary
questions.explanation: You need trail at the PREDECESSOR of the nth-from-end node (to do trail.next = trail.next.next). If lead is n+1 ahead of trail, when lead reaches null (one past the end), trail is n+1 nodes from the end — that is the (n+1)th from end = the predecessor of the nth from end. Advancing only n steps would land trail at the nth-from-end node itself (cannot delete without predecessor).

questions.question: You remove the 2nd from end of [1,2,3,4,5] (answer: 4, result [1,2,3,5]). Trace: after advancing lead 3 steps, where is lead?
options: At node 4
At node 3
At node 3 (1-indexed) — dummy(0)→1→2→3 is 3 steps from dummy
At node 5
questions.explanation: Start: lead=dummy. Step 1: lead=node1. Step 2: lead=node2. Step 3: lead=node3. Lead is at node 3. Now advance both until lead=null: lead=4,trail=1; lead=5,trail=2; lead=null,trail=3. Trail is at node3 (predecessor of node4). trail.next=trail.next.next removes node4. Correct.

questions.question: You use lead and trail starting from dummy. The list is [1] and n=1 (remove the only node). After advancing lead n+1=2 steps, where is lead?
options: At node 1
At null — 2 steps from dummy: step1=node1, step2=null
Beyond the list
At the dummy node itself
questions.explanation: From dummy: step1=node1, step2=null (node1.next=null). Lead=null. The while(lead) loop never executes — trail stays at dummy. trail.next=trail.next.next: dummy.next=node1.next=null. Returns dummy.next=null (empty list). This is exactly correct: removing the only node gives an empty list, handled without any special case.

coding_quest.title: Remove Nth Node From End
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement removeNthFromEnd(head, n) in one pass using two-pointer spacing with a dummy head. Advance lead n+1 steps, then move both until lead=null. Trail is then at the predecessor. Test all edge cases: middle removal, head removal (n=list length), and single-node list.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Advancing lead only n steps (not n+1). This lands trail at the target node itself when lead reaches the last node — but you need trail at the PREDECESSOR to perform trail.next = trail.next.next.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n) time but deletes the wrong node — removes the node AFTER the target instead of the target

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space — one pass.

hints.text: for(let i=0;i<=n;i++) lead=lead.next — this runs n+1 times. Why i<=n not i<n: i=0,1,...,n is n+1 iterations. After this loop, lead is n+1 steps ahead of trail (both started at dummy). When lead=null, trail is at the predecessor.

Why n+1 not n: after n steps, trail would be at the target node itself (not predecessor). You cannot do trail.next=trail.next.next to remove trail. With n+1 steps, trail is one node before the target — exactly where deletion needs it.
for(let i=0;i<=n;i++)lead=lead.next; while(lead){lead=lead.next;trail=trail.next;} trail.next=trail.next.next; return dummy.next;

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson advance `lead` exactly n+1 steps (not n steps) before starting the synchronized two-pointer movement?
options: n+1 is an arbitrary choice; n steps would work identically

The goal is for `trail` to land on the PREDECESSOR of the nth-from-end node (not on the target itself), so the deletion `trail.next = trail.next.next` can bypass the target — advancing lead n+1 steps (creating a gap of n+1 between lead and trail) means when lead reaches null, trail is exactly n+1 positions behind null, which is the predecessor of the nth-from-end node; advancing only n steps would leave trail AT the target node itself, with no predecessor access
n+1 advances are needed because the list is 1-indexed, not 0-indexed
The extra step compensates for the dummy head node's position
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's explicit reasoning: 'Off-by-one: advance n+1 steps (not n) to land on predecessor... trail must be at predecessor, not at target' — the deletion mechanism requires trail.next to be the target (so trail.next.next can skip it), which means trail itself must be one step BEFORE the target; n+1 steps of gap achieves this.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `removeNthFromEnd([1,2,3,4,5], n=2)` per the lesson's own trace. After the n+1=3 lead-advance and the synchronized movement, what is trail pointing to, and what deletion is performed?
options: trail points to node 4; node 4 is deleted

trail points to node 3 (the predecessor of node 4, the 2nd from end) — the lesson's trace confirms: after advancing lead 3 steps to node 3, then moving both until lead=null: lead goes 4→5→null, trail goes 1→2→3; trail ends at node 3, so trail.next (node 4) is removed via trail.next = trail.next.next (3→5), producing [1,2,3,5]
trail points to node 2; node 3 is deleted
The algorithm removes node 5 (the last node) for n=2
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace, confirmed by direct execution: 'Advance lead 3 steps (n+1=3): lead at node 3. Move both until lead=null: lead=4, trail=1; lead=5, trail=2; lead=null, trail=3. trail is predecessor of 4. trail.next = trail.next.next -> 3->5. Return [1,2,3,5]'.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `removeNthFromEnd([1], n=1)` per the lesson's own analysis. Why does the algorithm correctly handle this case (removing the only/head node)?
options: The algorithm fails on single-element lists and throws an error

With the dummy head, lead starts at dummy and advances n+1=2 steps: step i=0 → lead=node1, step i=1 → lead=null; the `while(lead)` loop immediately doesn't execute (lead is already null), leaving trail at dummy; then `dummy.next = dummy.next.next = null` removes node1, and `return dummy.next = null` correctly returns an empty list — confirmed by direct execution
The algorithm returns [1] unchanged for single-element lists
n=1 only works when the list has exactly 2 elements
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's own trace and confirmed by direct execution: the dummy head ensures trail starts there as a valid predecessor for even the head node — advancing lead n+1 steps past the dummy makes lead reach null immediately after the loop, leaving trail at dummy which then deletes the single real node in one pointer update.

syntax_mcq.question: In `for (let i = 0; i <= n; i++) { lead = lead.next; }`, why does the loop condition use `i <= n` rather than `i < n`?
options: i <= n and i < n produce the same number of iterations

`i <= n` iterates for i = 0, 1, 2, ..., n — that's n+1 total iterations, advancing lead n+1 steps; `i < n` would iterate for i = 0, 1, ..., n-1 — only n total iterations, advancing lead n steps; n+1 advances are specifically required (as established by the logic question) to land trail at the predecessor rather than the target itself
i <= n is only valid when n is an even number
The loop iterates exactly n times regardless of the condition used
syntax_mcq.explanation: `i <= n` produces n+1 iterations (0 through n inclusive), advancing lead exactly n+1 times — the exact count needed to create the correct gap; `i < n` would produce only n iterations (one too few), landing trail at the target instead of its predecessor and making the deletion incorrect.

coding_challenges.title: Remove Nth From End and Generalized Pointer-Spacing Toolkit
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement removeNthFromEnd matching the lesson exactly, then generalize the pointer-spacing pattern to find (without removing) the kth-from-end node.
requirements: Implement `removeNthFromEndImpl(head, n)` matching the lesson's dummy-head + spacing approach exactly
Implement `findKthFromEnd(head, k)` returning the VALUE of the kth node from the end (1-indexed) using the same spacing technique, or -1 if k exceeds the list length
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: removeNthFromEndImpl: O(n) one-pass, O(1) space. findKthFromEnd: O(n) one-pass, O(1) space. Both exploit the pointer-spacing pattern to achieve single-traversal solutions.

hints.text: removeNthFromEndImpl: advance lead n+1 times (i <= n loop condition), then move both until lead is null, giving trail at the predecessor; set trail.next = trail.next.next.
findKthFromEnd: advance lead k steps first (returning -1 if lead falls off the list — k exceeds length); then move both until lead is null, leaving trail at the kth-from-end node.
findKthFromEnd uses k steps advance (not k+1) because you want trail AT the target node, not its predecessor — this is the 1-step difference from removeNthFromEnd.

lessons.title: LRU Cache Design
lessons.objective: Design an LRU Cache with O(1) get and put using a doubly linked list and hash map, and articulate why both data structures are necessary.
concepts: LRU Cache definition: evict the least recently used item when capacity is full
O(1) get: hash map lookup by key
O(1) put: insert at front (most recent), evict from back (least recent)
O(1) move-to-front on get: doubly linked list remove + insert at front
Why doubly linked list: O(1) delete given node reference (from hash map)
Why hash map: O(1) key lookup to find the node reference
The combination: hash map gives the node, DLL enables O(1) restructuring
Sentinel head and tail: eliminate boundary conditions
lessons.explanation: An LRU Cache holds a maximum of capacity items. When a new item is added and the cache is full, the least recently used item is evicted. Both get and put must run in O(1). The data structure combination: a hash map (key -> DLL node) and a doubly linked list (maintains recency order). The DLL is ordered from most recently used (just after dummy head) to least recently used (just before dummy tail). Get: look up key in hash map O(1), get the node reference, move that node to the front of the DLL O(1) with doubly linked list, return the value. Put: if key exists, update value and move to front. If key is new and cache is full, remove the node at the back of the DLL (least recently used) and delete its key from the hash map, both O(1). Then insert the new node at the front and add to the hash map. Why doubly linked list and not singly: O(1) move-to-front requires O(1) delete of any node. Singly linked list delete requires O(n) predecessor search. Doubly linked list delete is O(1) because node.prev gives the predecessor directly.
lessons.analogy: An LRU Cache is a VIP lounge with a capacity limit. The most recently used guest is at the front of the lounge. The list behind them is in order of last use. When a new guest arrives and the lounge is full, the guest who has been there the longest without being touched (back of the list) is asked to leave. When any guest is used (visited), they jump to the front. The hash map is the guest list that tells the bouncer immediately where any specific guest is standing without walking through the whole lounge.

code_example.explanation: The LRUNode stores both key and val. The key is needed for map.delete(lru.key) during eviction. If only val were stored, we would not know which map entry to delete when evicting the LRU node. This key-in-node detail is the most commonly forgotten implementation detail in LRU Cache interviews.

common_mistakes: Not storing the key inside the LRU node — when evicting the LRU node (tail.prev), you need to delete it from the map; without the key stored in the node, you cannot do this deletion
Using a singly linked list instead of doubly linked list — _remove requires O(1) deletion of any node; singly linked list cannot do this without the predecessor, which requires O(n) traversal
Not checking if the key already exists in put before creating a new node — if the key exists, you must update the existing node and move it to front, not create a duplicate entry
lessons.interview_relevance: LRU Cache (#146) is Blind 75 and one of the most asked design problems at every company. It is used at senior interviews to test data structure composition and system design thinking. The expected answer requires both a hash map and a doubly linked list, with a clear explanation of why each is necessary. Candidates who suggest only a Map with insertion-order iteration are penalised for not knowing that Map.delete + Map.set destroys insertion order.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement LRUCache above and run all the test cases. Then extend it to an LFU Cache (Least Frequently Used): when the cache is full, evict the least frequently used item. Ties in frequency are broken by LRU. Research LeetCode #460 LFU Cache. This requires frequency buckets (a Map of frequency -> doubly linked list of nodes at that frequency) and is a Level 2 problem — attempt it to see how far your current toolkit takes you.

visual_explanation.description: Draw the LRU Cache after put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3). Two structures side by side. Left: Map {1:nodeA, 3:nodeC} (key 2 evicted). Right: DLL: head-sentinel ⟷ nodeC(3) ⟷ nodeA(1) ⟷ tail-sentinel. Show arrows from map keys to their nodes in the DLL. Annotate: 'HEAD=MRU, TAIL=LRU'. Show the eviction step: put(3,3) when full — tail.prev=nodeB(2), remove nodeB from DLL, delete key 2 from map, insert nodeC at front. Draw the 4 pointer updates for insertFront. Callout: 'The key stored in each node (nodeB.key=2) is what enables map.delete(2) during eviction'.

interview_war_story.story: LRU Cache. The candidate implemented it correctly except they did not store the key in the node. Their test sequence ran fine until eviction: put(3,3) should evict key 2. Their code called map.delete(lru.key) where lru.key was undefined. The map was never cleaned up. On the next get(2), map.has(2) was still true and returned a garbage node. The interviewer asked 'What is the state of your map after eviction?' The candidate traced and saw map still contained key 2. 'I need to store the key in the node so I can delete it from the map.' That insight — storing the key for reverse lookup — is the critical detail that separates a working LRU from a broken one. Hired after the fix.
interview_war_story.lesson: LRU Cache has one easily missed detail: store the key inside the LRUNode. During eviction you navigate from the DLL (tail.prev) to the node, then must find the key to delete from the map. Without key-in-node, this is impossible in O(1).

questions.question: Why does LRU Cache require BOTH a hash map AND a doubly linked list? Would either alone suffice?
options: Either alone would work

Hash map alone: O(1) get/put but cannot maintain recency order or evict LRU in O(1). DLL alone: O(1) reorder but O(n) lookup by key. Together: map gives O(1) key→node lookup, DLL gives O(1) reorder and eviction. Both are required for O(1) get/put.
A sorted array works instead
A single hash map with timestamps suffices
questions.explanation: Hash map alone can find any key in O(1) but cannot identify which key is least recently used without scanning all entries (O(n)). DLL alone maintains recency order but searching by key is O(n) traversal. Combined: hash map says 'key K is at node N in O(1)'; DLL moves N to front and removes from back in O(1). Each structure handles what the other cannot.

questions.question: In LRU Cache put, when a new key is inserted and the cache is full, which node is evicted and how?
options: A random node

The node just before the tail sentinel (tail.prev) — it is the least recently used. Remove it from DLL with O(1) deletion (using prev pointer), delete its key from the map using node.key, then insert the new node at the front.
The node just after the head sentinel
The oldest node by timestamp
questions.explanation: The DLL is ordered most-recently-used (front, after head sentinel) to least-recently-used (back, before tail sentinel). The LRU node is always tail.prev. O(1) deletion via node.prev and node.next pointers. map.delete(lruNode.key) removes it from the map — this requires the key to be stored in the node.

questions.question: In LRU Cache get, after finding the node from the map, what MUST you do before returning the value?
options: Nothing — just return node.val
Move the node to the front of the DLL (mark it as most recently used). Failure to do this means recently accessed items are not properly protected from eviction.
Delete the node from the map
Increment the node's access count
questions.explanation: Get is a use of the key — the key is now the most recently used. You must move its node to the front of the DLL. Without this, the node stays in its old position and may be evicted despite being recently used. The two-step get: map.get(key) → get node, then remove(node) + insertFront(node) → update recency.

coding_quest.title: LRU Cache — Full Implementation
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement LRUCache(capacity) with get(key) and put(key, val), both O(1). Use sentinel head and tail nodes. Run the full test sequence from the problem description. Explain why the key must be stored in the node.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Not storing the key in the node. During eviction (tail.prev), you need to call map.delete(lruNode.key) but if key is not in the node, you cannot identify which map entry to remove.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: Correct DLL operations but broken map — cannot evict properly without stored key

optimal_solution.complexity: get and put: O(1). Space O(capacity) for map + DLL nodes.

hints.text: get: const node=this.map.get(key); this._remove(node); this._insertFront(node); return node.val. put (new key): create node, _insertFront, map.set(key,node). put (existing key): get node, change val, _remove, _insertFront. put (new + full): evict this.tail.prev — _remove(lru), map.delete(lru.key).

The eviction order: remove LRU from DLL first (_remove), then delete from map (map.delete(lru.key)). The key stored in the node is what makes map.delete work. Without it, you have the node reference but no key to delete from the map.
Eviction: const lru=this.tail.prev; this._remove(lru); this.map.delete(lru.key); Then: const node=new LRUNode(key,val); this._insertFront(node); this.map.set(key,node);

theory_mcq.question: Why are BOTH a doubly linked list AND a hash map necessary for an O(1) LRU Cache — and why is neither data structure sufficient alone?
options: A hash map alone is sufficient for O(1) LRU cache; the DLL is redundant

The hash map alone enables O(1) KEY LOOKUP but provides no ordering information (can't determine which entry is least recently used) and no O(1) deletion-by-position; the DLL alone maintains O(1) ordering and O(1) delete-given-node but has no O(1) key-based lookup (would require O(n) search). Together: hash map finds the node in O(1), DLL stores the node reference and enables O(1) reordering and O(1) eviction from the LRU end — each structure compensates for the other's weakness
The DLL alone is sufficient; the hash map just speeds up lookup slightly
Neither structure achieves O(1); the best possible is O(log n)
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit reasoning: 'Why doubly linked list: O(1) delete given node reference (from hash map)' and 'Why hash map: O(1) key lookup to find the node reference' — the combination is necessary because: the map gives fast lookup and stores the node reference, the DLL uses that node reference for O(1) restructuring (reorder, evict), neither alone providing both capabilities simultaneously.

theory_mcq.question: In `LRUCache.get(key)`, why is a 'cache hit' NOT simply returning the cached value — why must `_remove` and `_insertFront` also be called?
options: get() only needs to return the value; the DLL manipulation is unnecessary

Returning the value is only HALF the semantic contract of an LRU Cache: a GET operation marks the accessed item as MOST RECENTLY USED — failing to move it to the front would leave it at its old (potentially LRU-end-approaching) position, risking its eviction before items that haven't been accessed as recently; `_remove + _insertFront` (move-to-front) is what implements the 'recently used' part of 'Least Recently Used'
move-to-front is only required when capacity is exceeded
get() already returns the correct value without DLL manipulation on cache hits
theory_mcq.explanation: LRU semantics require that every access (get OR put) marks the item as most recently used — without the move-to-front, a frequently-accessed item that happened to be inserted early could drift toward the LRU end and be incorrectly evicted; the `_remove + _insertFront` pair atomically repositions the item to the MRU end, correctly maintaining the usage ordering.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the lesson's LRU Cache test sequence: `put(1,1); put(2,2); get(1); put(3,3); get(2)`. What does `get(2)` return, and which key was evicted during `put(3,3)`?
options: get(2) returns 2 and key 1 was evicted

get(2) returns -1 and key 2 was evicted — after put(1,1) and put(2,2) the cache is full [2(MRU)→1(LRU)]; get(1) moves 1 to front [1(MRU)→2(LRU)]; put(3,3) evicts the LRU which is now 2 (not 1, since get(1) refreshed it), leaving [3(MRU)→1]; get(2) misses (2 was evicted), returning -1 — confirmed by direct execution
get(2) returns 2 because eviction only happens after capacity+1 operations
Both get(2) and get(1) return -1 since all entries are evicted by put(3,3)
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact test output, confirmed by direct execution: `cache.get(2); // -1 — 2 was evicted` — the key insight is that `get(1)` moved key 1 to the MRU position BEFORE `put(3,3)` needed to evict, making key 2 the LRU at eviction time, not key 1.

logic_mcq.question: In `LRUCache.put(key, val)`, why is it important that the evicted LRU node stores its KEY (not just its value), and where is this design evident in the LRUNode class?
options: The key is not stored in the node; it's looked up from the map during eviction

During eviction, `this.map.delete(lru.key)` must remove the evicted entry from the hash map — if the node only stored its value (not its key), there would be no way to identify WHICH map entry to delete without a full O(n) map scan; storing `this.key = key` in LRUNode provides O(1) map deletion during eviction, confirmed by the lesson's explicit comment: 'remove from map using stored key'
The key is stored only for debugging purposes, not for functional correctness
Keys are always 0 or 1, so no explicit storage is needed
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit code comment: 'this.map.delete(lru.key); // remove from map using stored key' — during eviction, we have the LRU node reference (from tail.prev) but need its KEY to delete from the map; since the map is keyed by the original key (not by node reference), the node must store its own key for this O(1) reverse-lookup during eviction.

syntax_mcq.question: In `_insertFront(node)`, why must `this.head.next.prev = node` be set BEFORE `this.head.next = node`?
options: Order doesn't matter; both assignments are independent

If `this.head.next = node` were done first, `this.head.next` would immediately refer to the newly-inserted `node` — then `this.head.next.prev = node` would set `node.prev = node` (self-reference/cycle), rather than correctly setting the OLD first real node's prev to point to the new node; doing `this.head.next.prev = node` first (while head.next still refers to the OLD front node) correctly makes the old front node point back to the new node before head.next is overwritten
this.head.next.prev and this.head.next are the same assignment
The order only matters when the list is completely empty
syntax_mcq.explanation: Pointer assignment order is critical for DLL operations: `this.head.next.prev = node` must execute while `this.head.next` still refers to the OLD front node (making it look back at the new node); if head.next were updated first, `this.head.next.prev` would refer to the new node itself, creating a self-loop — four-pointer DLL insertions always require careful ordering.

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: get: O(1) — hash map lookup + O(1) DLL remove + O(1) DLL insert. put: O(1) — hash map operations + O(1) DLL operations. All operations are O(1) due to the DLL + hash map combination.

hints.text: _insertFront: set node.next and node.prev first, then update the existing neighbors — critically, set head.next.prev = node BEFORE head.next = node to avoid a self-reference.
get: handle miss (return -1) first, then remove the node from its current position and reinsert at front before returning its value.
put with eviction: evict by getting tail.prev (the LRU node), calling _remove, and deleting from the map using lru.key — only then insert the new node at front and add to the map.

lessons.title: Linked List Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Given any linked list problem, apply the correct technique within 60 seconds: pointer manipulation, two-pointer pattern, dummy head, or data structure combination.
concepts: Linked list technique decision tree
Pointer manipulation: reversal, insertion, deletion
Two-pointer patterns: fast-slow, spacing, same-direction
Dummy head: always use when head itself may change
Data structure combination: DLL + hash map for O(1) operations
Visualisation: draw the list before coding any pointer change
Module 6 Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 problems mapped
Skills unlocked: Linked Lists, Two Pointers (linked), LRU Cache
lessons.explanation: Linked list problems decompose into four technique categories. Pointer manipulation: the problem requires restructuring the list — reversal, merging, removing nodes. Always use a dummy head, always draw the before and after pointer state before coding. Two-pointer patterns: fast-slow for middle and cycle detection; spacing for kth-from-end and removal; same-direction for in-place operations. Data structure combination: when a linked list alone gives O(n) for a required O(1) operation, combine with a hash map (LRU Cache) or another structure. Visualisation is not optional: linked list pointer bugs are invisible in your head and visible on paper. Draw every node as a box with arrows. Draw the state before and after every pointer change. Code from the drawing. The most common linked list mistakes — losing a pointer, wrong order of assignments, off-by-one in two-pointer spacing — are all immediately visible in a drawing and invisible in mental simulation.
lessons.analogy: Linked list problem thinking is like plumbing. You cannot see water flow in your head accurately enough to be sure the pipes are connected correctly. Draw the pipe diagram, label every connection, then connect the pipes in the drawn order. If you skip the diagram and connect by intuition, you will create a leak (pointer loss) or a backflow (cycle) somewhere. Experienced plumbers still draw diagrams for complex jobs.

code_example.explanation: Seven Blind 75 problems are unlocked by Module 6. Completing all seven is the measurable outcome of this module. The progression: start with #206 (reversal, simplest), then #21 (merge, dummy head), then #141 (cycle, fast-slow), then #19 (spacing), then #143 (reorder, combines fast-slow + reversal), then #23 (merge k, hardest technical), then #146 (LRU, hardest design). This ordering builds on each technique before combining them.

common_mistakes: Not drawing the pointer state before coding — every experienced developer draws linked list diagrams; skipping this step because it feels slow is how pointer bugs get introduced that take 20 minutes to debug

Trying to manipulate pointers mentally in the order they need to change without a drawing — the correct order of pointer assignments (e.g., in insertion: newNode.next before prev.next) is only obvious from a diagram

Moving to Module 7 (Trees) before completing Module 6 Blind 75 problems — trees use many of the same recursive and pointer patterns as linked lists; completing linked list problems first makes tree problems significantly more approachable
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 6 has the most Blind 75 problems of any module in Level 1. Seven problems including LRU Cache (the most asked design problem at FAANG) and Merge K Sorted Lists (the hardest Blind 75 problem in this module). Solving all seven fluently with correct complexity analysis is the clearest signal that a candidate is ready for mid-level technical screens.
lessons.mini_challenge: Set a 105-minute timer (15 minutes each) and solve these seven Blind 75 problems in order: #206 Reverse Linked List, #21 Merge Two Sorted Lists, #141 Linked List Cycle, #19 Remove Nth Node From End, #143 Reorder List, #23 Merge K Sorted Lists, #146 LRU Cache. For each: apply the 5-step framework, draw the pointer state on paper before coding, state time and space complexity. Journal your results. Re-solve any incomplete problems in 3 days.

visual_explanation.description: Draw a decision flowchart for linked list problems. Root: 'What does the problem require?' Four branches: Branch 1 'Restructure/reorder' → POINTER MANIPULATION (dummy head, draw before coding). Examples: Reverse List, Merge Sorted, Remove All Occurrences. Branch 2 'Middle / palindrome / cycle' → FAST-SLOW POINTER. Examples: Find Middle, Palindrome, Cycle Detection. Branch 3 'Kth from end / remove nth' → POINTER SPACING. Examples: Remove Nth, Find Kth. Branch 4 'O(1) lookup + O(1) eviction' → DLL + HASH MAP. Examples: LRU Cache. Below each branch: key complexity (time + space). Footer: 'Module 6 = 7 Blind 75 problems. Drawing pointer diagrams is not optional.'

interview_war_story.story: The candidate was given 4 linked list problems back to back with 15 minutes each. They started coding #206 immediately without drawing. After 8 minutes, they had a bug: their reversal returned the wrong pointer. They spent 4 more minutes debugging what a 30-second diagram would have caught. On #21 they drew the list first: 2 minutes drawing, 5 minutes coding, correct on first run. On #141 they drew again: caught the 'check before moving' bug in the drawing. On #19 they drew the spacing: n+1 steps was obvious from the diagram. Final score: problem 1 took 12 minutes (bug + debug), problems 2-4 took 8 minutes each (draw + code). Interviewer noted: 'I noticed you started drawing from problem 2 — that made your solutions dramatically faster and correct the first time.' Hired.
interview_war_story.lesson: Drawing linked list diagrams takes 2 minutes and saves 10-20 minutes of debugging. From problem 2 onward in any linked list interview, draw first. The diagram makes correct pointer assignment order obvious. Without it, you are guessing at pointer order and debugging mistakes.

questions.question: A problem says 'in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, find the middle of a linked list.' Which technique?
options: Traverse once to count, traverse again to middle — O(n) but two passes
Fast-slow pointer — fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1 step. When fast reaches end, slow is at middle. Single pass, O(1) space.
Hash map of indices
Convert to array
questions.explanation: Fast-slow pointer: one pass, no extra memory. Linear scan for length + second scan: two passes, still O(n) but less elegant and interviewers specifically ask for one-pass O(1). The single-pointer-pair solution is the expected answer for any 'one pass O(1)' linked list constraint.

questions.question: A problem requires 'O(1) get and put for a cache with LRU eviction policy.' Which data structure combination?
options: Array + binary search
Hash map + doubly linked list — map gives O(1) key lookup to node, DLL gives O(1) reorder (via prev pointer) and O(1) eviction from back
Priority queue
Singly linked list + hash map
questions.explanation: The two requirements: (1) O(1) key lookup → hash map. (2) O(1) reorder + O(1) eviction → doubly linked list (prev pointer enables O(1) delete any node). Singly linked list cannot delete any node in O(1). Priority queue gives O(log n) eviction. Hash map + DLL is the canonical O(1) LRU solution.

questions.question: A problem gives you a linked list and asks you to draw the pointer state before coding. A colleague says 'drawing is wasting time in a timed interview.' Who is right?
options: The colleague — skip drawing, code faster

You — drawing saves time overall. Linked list pointer bugs take 10-20 minutes to debug without a diagram. The 2-3 minutes spent drawing eliminates the bug entirely. Net time saved is 7-17 minutes. Professional engineers always draw linked list diagrams for non-trivial problems.
It depends on experience
Drawing is optional for easy problems
questions.explanation: Every linked list expert draws diagrams for non-trivial problems. The 2-3 minute drawing investment pays off because: (1) pointer assignment order becomes obvious from the drawing (cannot get correct order without it), (2) bugs are visible in the diagram before writing code, (3) interviewers see you think systematically. Net result: less total time, correct code on first attempt.

coding_quest.title: Pattern Sprint: 4 Blind 75 Linked List Problems
coding_quest.problem_statement: Solve four Blind 75 linked list problems back to back. For each: (1) state the technique, (2) draw pointer state on paper before coding, (3) implement in under 15 lines, (4) state time and space. Problems: #206 Reverse Linked List, #21 Merge Two Sorted Lists, #141 Linked List Cycle, #19 Remove Nth Node From End.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Not drawing pointer diagrams before coding leads to pointer assignment order bugs. reverseList returning curr instead of prev. mergeTwoLists missing curr.next=l1||l2. hasCycle checking equality before moving. removeNthFromEnd advancing n steps instead of n+1.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n) but returns null — returning wrong pointer

optimal_solution.complexity: All: O(n) time. reverseList/hasCycle/removeNthFromEnd: O(1) space. mergeTwoLists: O(1) extra space.

hints.text: Name technique first: (1) 3-pointer reversal, (2) dummy head + compare, (3) fast-slow check-after-move, (4) dummy + n+1 spacing. Then draw. Then code.

reverseList: const next=curr.next before curr.next=prev. Return prev (not curr). mergeTwoLists: always append curr.next=l1||l2 after while loop. hasCycle: check after moving both pointers. removeNthFromEnd: i<=n gives n+1 steps.

All four are implementable from the pattern descriptions. The most error-prone lines: reverseList returns prev; mergeTwoLists ends with curr.next=l1||l2; hasCycle checks equality after advance; removeNthFromEnd uses i<=n (n+1 iterations).

theory_mcq.question: Per the lesson's decision tree, what are the five main technique categories for linked list problems, and what signal words point to each?
options: There is only one technique: pointer manipulation

The lesson identifies: (1) Pointer Manipulation — signals 'reverse', 'reorder'; (2) Fast-Slow Pointer — signals 'middle', 'palindrome'; (3) Floyd's (fast-slow + phase 2 reset) — signal 'cycle'; (4) Pointer Spacing — signals 'kth from end', 'remove nth from end'; (5) DLL + Hash Map — signal 'O(1) get/put/evict'
All linked list problems use the same fast-slow pointer approach
The decision tree only applies to singly linked lists, not doubly linked ones
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact decision tree comments: each technique maps to specific problem signal words — 'Reverse'/'reorder' → pointer manipulation; 'Middle'/'palindrome' → fast-slow; 'Cycle' → Floyd's; 'kth from end'/'remove nth' → pointer spacing; 'O(1) get/put/evict' → DLL + hash map. Recognizing signal words in 60 seconds is the explicit objective.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson specifically recommend 'draw the list before coding any pointer change' as a key practical tip?
options: Drawing is required by interview protocols; it has no practical debugging benefit

Linked list pointer bugs are uniquely hard to detect mentally because a single wrong assignment can silently create a cycle, disconnect a portion of the list, or lose a node reference permanently — a physical diagram of nodes, arrows, and pointer updates makes it immediately visible whether each assignment correctly preserves all needed references before any old pointers are overwritten, catching the 'save next before reversing curr.next' class of bugs that are trivial to make but hard to spot in code alone
Drawing ensures the interviewer can see the thought process; correctness is secondary
Drawing is only helpful for lists with more than 10 nodes
theory_mcq.explanation: Linked list manipulation is notoriously error-prone because pointer overwrites are destructive and invisible — drawing the list with explicit arrow updates before coding makes the required operation sequence concrete and spatial, preventing the class of bugs (like losing a forward reference before saving it) that arise from reasoning about pointer state purely in the abstract.

logic_mcq.question: A problem states: 'Given a singly linked list, determine if it reads the same forwards and backwards.' Applying the lesson's decision tree, which technique applies, and why?
options: Floyd's cycle detection, because palindromes involve cycles

Fast-Slow Pointer — the signal word 'palindrome' directly maps to this category in the lesson's decision tree; the solution uses findMiddle (fast-slow) to split the list, reverses the second half (pointer manipulation), and compares the two halves from their respective heads
Pointer Spacing — kth-from-end comparisons are needed
DLL + Hash Map — storing and retrieving values for comparison
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact decision tree: "'Middle' or 'palindrome' -> FAST-SLOW POINTER... isPalindrome" — 'palindrome' is explicitly listed as a fast-slow signal word, and the isPalindrome algorithm from L5 directly uses fast-slow to find the middle, demonstrating the pattern.

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's Module 6 Blind75 problem map, how many problems are marked `blind75: true`, and which pattern appears most frequently among them?
options: 4 problems are Blind75; the most common pattern is Floyd's cycle detection

7 problems are marked blind75:true (ids 206, 21, 143, 19, 141, 23, 146) — confirmed by direct execution; no single pattern dominates exclusively, but pointer manipulation (reversal #206), dummy head+merge (#21), and fast-slow variants (#143, #141) appear most prominently among the 7 Blind75 problems
All 10 problems in the list are Blind75
Only 3 problems are Blind75: the cycle detection ones
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: `module6_problems.filter(p => p.blind75).length` returns 7, and the 7 Blind75 entries span: Reverse Linked List (pointer manipulation), Merge Two Sorted Lists (dummy head+merge), Reorder List (fast-slow+reverse), Remove Nth Node (pointer spacing), Linked List Cycle (Floyd's Phase 1), Merge K Sorted Lists (divide-and-conquer), and LRU Cache (DLL+hash map).

syntax_mcq.question: In the module6_problems array, why does each object store both `pattern` (a string) AND `blind75` (a boolean) as separate fields, rather than combining them?
options: They could be combined; the separation is purely stylistic

The two fields serve orthogonal purposes: `pattern` is a CATEGORICAL LABEL identifying the algorithmic technique needed (useful for filtering by technique or understanding the approach), while `blind75` is a MEMBERSHIP FLAG indicating whether this specific problem appears on a particular canonical interview problem set — these are independent dimensions, and keeping them separate allows filtering by either dimension independently (e.g., all fast-slow problems, or all Blind75 problems, or both simultaneously)
pattern is required by JavaScript objects; blind75 is optional
Combining them would make the array too large for JavaScript to handle
syntax_mcq.explanation: Orthogonal attributes should be stored as separate fields — `pattern` answers 'what technique does this problem use?' while `blind75` answers 'is this on the Blind75 list?'; these are independent questions and combining them (e.g., 'blind75-pointer-manipulation') would make filtering by only one dimension impossible and the data model harder to query.
